documents.abstract: Tourists abroad routinely face short, consequential service encounters: an inflated taxi fare, a pharmacy visit in an unfamiliar language, a room that does not match the booking. Research on generative artificial intelligence (AI) in tourism has concentrated on how such systems help travellers plan, choose and delegate decisions, and on how AI support during a trip shapes confidence and satisfaction. Separately, research in language education, health-professions education and workplace training shows that rehearsal with simulated counterparts can build skills, although transfer of those skills to real settings is conditional rather than automatic. This conceptual article brings these streams together for the tourist. It proposes the AI-Assisted Travel Rehearsal (ATR) model, an iterative cycle in which travellers rehearse anticipated encounters with general-purpose conversational AI before and during a trip, receive minimal AI support in real encounters, and reflect on each encounter to plan the next rehearsal. Drawing on social cognitive theory, experiential learning theory, the transactional model of stress and coping, scaffolding and fading, and transfer-of-training research, the article specifies a mechanism linking rehearsal to mastery experience, situational self-efficacy and behavioural capability, conditional transfer, and progressive AI fading. Its central claim, the Self-Fading AI Hypothesis, holds that well-designed AI support should reduce travellers' reliance on AI in real encounters without loss of independent performance; reduced AI use alone is not treated as evidence of autonomy. The article states six propositions with explicit conditions of support, identifies which can be tested confirmatorily, and proposes a randomised, actively controlled classroom experiment with AI-unavailable and AI-available transfer tasks, followed by a multilevel field study of first-time international travellers. No empirical results are reported.
keywords: transactional model of stress and coping

documents.abstract: The inherent complexity and exposure of projects to disruptive events during the formulation, planning, and execution stages necessitate the adoption of technological tools that optimize the processes underlying these stages and, consequently, support decision-making. In this context, this research project aims to identify opportunities for applying AI to key project planning activities. To this end, a literature review was conducted using both qualitative and quantitative evidence, resulting in the selection and analysis of 51 academic articles. Similarly, the PMI, ISO 21502, IPMA, and PRINCE2 standards were examined to generate a unified framework for the main planning activities. The results revealed AI applications in semantic analysis, predictive analytics, optimization algorithms, automation, and workflow integration. Technologies such as language models, generative artificial intelligence, machine learning, reinforcement learning, and AI agents were also analyzed. These technologies enabled the reduction of repetitive tasks, improved accuracy in deviation detection, and thus optimized project planning. It was demonstrated that AI can strengthen and enhance the performance of key project planning activities.

Productive task time is a core concern of human-performance and work-system design, and construction vocational students are forming the time-use habits they will bring into the workforce. This study examined how social media use intensity, and its attention, absorption, duration, and frequency facets, is associated with academic procrastination among 117 randomly selected eleventh-grade Building Modeling and Information Design (DPIB) students at a public vocational high school in Bandung, Indonesia. Confirmatory factor analysis showed that reverse-keyed items loaded near zero on their constructs; the retained items had composite reliabilities of .74–.89 and discriminant validity (HTMT < .85). Intensity was high (67.59%) and procrastination moderate (54.78%). Intensity was positively associated with procrastination (β = .444, 95% CI for B [0.189, 0.415], R² = .197), and the association held with CFA-refined scales (β = .409) and after excluding influential cases. Duration dominated the facets, accounting for 63.5% of the explained variance (bootstrap 95% CI 44.1–74.0%), whereas attention, absorption, and frequency added no significant unique prediction. A sensitivity analysis indicated that an unmeasured confounder would need correlations of at least .565 with both variables to overturn the inference. Because the design is cross-sectional, the results indicate association rather than causation. They support measurable time-allocation interventions: device-free work blocks, milestone-based project scheduling, and self-regulation guidance.

People often avoid speaking up not because they lack ideas, but because voice feels socially risky. We examine whether and how state authenticity—the feeling of alignment with one’s true self—influences challenging voice. Across five experimental studies (four preregistered) spanning field and laboratory samples ( N = 2,195), we manipulate state authenticity and test its relationship with challenging voice. Findings suggest that state authenticity can facilitate challenging voice, with effects emerging either directly or indirectly through increased subjective agency. The agency pathway remained evident when self-presentational concern was modeled simultaneously (Study 3b) and was stronger among individuals lower in extraversion, higher in agreeableness, and higher in dispositional authenticity (Study 4). Drawing on self-determination and self-transcendence perspectives, we argue that authentic states can shift regulation toward internally endorsed action, helping individuals act on their convictions despite interpersonal risk. These findings clarify how and for whom authenticity translates into challenging interpersonal communication.

documents.abstract: Although building energy modelling (BEM) effectively identifies sources of energy waste, it is a time-consuming, manual, and costly solution. Generative AI, specifically large language models (LLMs), could expedite BEM, but studies have not extensively validated the technology with users. Our study compares effectiveness, time, and usability for 13 non-experts modelling a complex BEM task using both traditional and template-guided LLM workflows. We analyse participants' models, survey responses, and screen activity. For effectiveness, the template-guided workflow results in fewer failed tasks but no significant gains in accuracy. For time, the traditional method is faster for three out of five modelling stages, with one reaching statistical significance. For usability, users overall prefer the template-guided workflow and rate it higher in satisfaction, perceived accuracy, and learnability, especially for more open-ended tasks. These findings indicate that generative AI could improve BEM usability and thereby ultimately enhance access and adoption of building energy modelling.

For over half a decade, the Abstraction and Reasoning Corpus has played a critical role in evaluating the fluid intelligence and skill acquisition efficiency of machine learning systems. While the dataset has proven especially useful in advancing program synthesis, few investments have been made in distilling the transformational logic of these tasks into their most irreducible computational forms. In conjunction with the NeurIPS 2025 Competition Track, we organized the 2025 Google Code Golf Championship, a three-month online challenge designed to elicit minimal Python solutions for all training puzzles in the seminal ARC-AGI-1 benchmark suite. Sponsored by Google DeepMind and funded with $100,000 in prizes, the contest attracted over 1,000 teams and yielded tens of thousands of verified, open-source programs that collectively establish tight upper bounds on the Kolmogorov complexity of each task. In this paper, we offer a comprehensive retrospective of the event, including an overview of the contest format, a survey of approaches taken by top teams, and a discussion of potential implications for the future design of intelligent agents.

Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly being used in various clinical settings to support clinical reasoning and decision-making. Although they have demonstrated strong performance on medical knowledge and reasoning tasks, and early studies suggest potential to reduce medical errors, emerging evidence also highlights important safety concerns, including clinically significant management errors in outputs that may not be readily apparent to users. How these tools can be integrated into clinical practice to consistently lead to improved patient outcomes remains an open question. AI-assisted reasoning unfolds across a sequence of decisions: whether to use AI for the clinical question, how to engage with the tool, how to interpret its output, and whether to act. Each stage in this sequence introduces distinct risks, including inappropriate tool selection, incomplete or biased inputs, overconfidence in fluent responses, and failure to recognize error or appreciate nuance. These risks are further shaped by the same clinician factors that generally affect clinical reasoning such as experience, workload, and uncertainty management. Viewing the AI-clinician interaction as a process rather than a single moment highlights several key points of vulnerability but also opportunities for training. Ultimately, the safe use of AI may depend less on the quality of the model and more on the clinician’s ability to recognize when its outputs should be questioned, verified, or set aside.

documents.abstract: A polished assignment can conceal who chose the method, weighed the evidence and reached the conclusion, which makes a student’s independent reasoning difficult to assess. Drawing on the metacognitive account of cognitive offloading and Social Cognitive Theory, this qualitative study examined how reliance on generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) relates to independent thinking, cognitive confidence and intellectual autonomy. Semi-structured online interviews were conducted with 22 undergraduate and postgraduate students, aged 20 to 29, from universities in Islamabad and Rawalpindi, Pakistan, each describing a recent academic episode involving GenAI. Thematic analysis traced when students sought assistance, which decisions they delegated and how they later justified their choices, and produced six themes. Delegating study planning preserved autonomy when students kept control over content, whereas removing a familiar AI prompt exposed difficulty in selecting a method despite earlier success with calculations. Confidence also diverged from accuracy: one student withheld a sound answer without AI confirmation, while another trusted a diagnosis because AI agreed with it, although both had missed the same error. Comparing drafts, checking sources and answering peers’ questions helped students identify assumptions and give reasons for revision. The findings support assessment practices that distinguish producing an answer with assistance from being able to explain or defend it without assistance.

Although robots show great potential as teammates, most researchers have focused on settings with a narrow view of possible human abilities, focusing on users without disabilities. Considering that verbal communication is one of the most widely used modalities in Human–Robot Interaction, its implications for teams composed of hearing and hard-of-hearing users remain underexplored. We set out to investigate this research gap by conducting an empirical study (N=16) in which a Tagi robot plays a collaborative game with two human participants, one is deaf or hard-of-hearing, and the other is hearing. We manipulated the communication modalities employed by the robot, verbal or non-verbal, in a within-subjects design. Our results showed that the verbal robot (compared to the non-verbal) sparked more non-verbal behaviours among participants, and that despite hearing participants perceived the robot as more animate and fair, deaf and hard of hearing participants felt more excluded. Finally, broader implications for social robots in mixed-hearing ability groups are discussed.

documents.abstract: The study aims to investigate the effect of AI Readiness, HRM Practices and Continuous Learning Culture to HR Analytics Capability in public sector enterprises in Indonesia. The research was conducted based on a quantitative approach and the survey technique. The research participants consisted of the workers of public sector organizations who have expertise in the use of digital information systems and management of personnel data. The data were collected using an online questionnaire through Google Forms. The questions used a five-point Likert scale. The sampling technique used purposive sampling. Multiple linear regression was used to explore HR Analytics Capability in relation to the three independent variables. The proposed study model indicates that AI Readiness, HRM Practices and Continuous Learning Culture are positively related to HR Analytics Capability. AI Readiness is expected to have the highest relative impact. Artificial intelligence preparation may enhance the organizational capacity to integrate, analyze and use personnel data. Quality information is available with good human resource management practices. Moreover, a culture of continuous learning promotes the enhancement of employees’ analytical skills, teamwork and flexibility. The report provides practical implications for public service companies in terms of the value of strengthening AI infrastructure, data quality, digital competences, human resource management practices and promoting a culture of continuous learning for achieving HR Analytics Capability.

Artificial intelligence (AI) has come a long way from its early theoretical days in the mid -1950s to become an advanced, data-based system that can learn from experience and execute jobs automatically. At present times, AI acts as a game-changer in education by making possible customized educational experiences based on the use of machine learning frameworks that provide individual guidance to every student, taking into account their speed, behaviour, preferences, and accomplishments. The change of this technological nature means that the role of a teacher must be shifted to the one who should now only provide guidance and help in, additionally, overseeing the machines. Beyond classrooms, AI adoption is a priority for national policies. For instance, India’s National Education Policy 2020 requires the teaching of AI and computational thinking in schools. The curriculum is set to start from Grade 3 in the academic year 2026-27. However, the rise of AI may create some challenges in terms of socio-economics. While AIED researchers are usually driven by the goals of enhancing learning results, the experience from other fields of AI indicates that good intentions do not guarantee ethical use of the technology. Important issues such as data ownership, algorithm bias, transparency, and student agency still remain unresolved. There is a necessity of collaborative endeavours in the creation of a community-wide framework in addressing the difference between "doing ethical things" and "doing things ethically. The PRISMA (Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses) framework is a prominent method for ensuring transparency and repeatability in systematic reviews and can be used in the mapping of the enormous literature in this evolving sphere, while the mentioned resources mainly rely on expert surveys of leading scientists to define the major shortcomings.

documents.abstract: This article examines how artificial intelligence affects teaching effectiveness in three areas: lesson preparation, instructional support during learning, and students’ independent performance. A comparative analysis of five international studies considers what each AI tool was designed to do, how it was used, and which outcomes were measured. In a school-based trial, teachers given access to ChatGPT and a practical guide spent less time preparing science lessons and materials. In mathematics tutoring, real-time AI support helped tutors ask more probing questions, and their students were more likely to master the topics covered. Research on AI tutoring also highlights the importance of assessing what students can do independently. In one mathematics experiment, unrestricted AI assistance improved performance during practice, but students scored lower than the control group when they later worked without the tool. An AI tutor that offered teacher-designed hints mitigated this effect. For pedagogical universities in Uzbekistan, the analysis identifies three priorities for preparing future teachers: reviewing AI-generated teaching materials, using AI to support questioning and feedback, and assessing what students can do without AI assistance.

documents.abstract: The research aims to determine the impact of artificial intelligence technologies on enhancing cybersecurity, by applying it to employees of telecommunications companies in Maysan Governorate, Iraq. The research was based on the descriptive analytical method, and the results showed the existence of strong significant correlations between artificial intelligence technologies and the dimensions of cybersecurity. The rapid integration of Generative Artificial Intelligence (GenAI) into workplaces is transforming not only how employees perform their tasks but also how they experience work. However, the implications of this transformation for sustainable development remain insufficiently understood, particularly regarding whether AI-enabled workplaces can support employees’ long-term well-being and resilience. Addressing this gap, this study examines how positive attitudes toward Generative AI (POS_ATT) and responsible AI signals (RAIS) contribute to multidimensional Green Well-being through employee engagement (ENG). Drawing on the Technology Acceptance Model, Signaling Theory, and the Job Demands–Resources theory, Green Well-being is conceptualized as a sustainable state encompassing emotional (GEW), cognitive (GCW), and social well-being (GSW). A quantitative cross-sectional survey was conducted among 342 knowledge workers employed by Vietnamese organizations using Generative AI. Participants were recruited using convenience and snowball sampling. The proposed model was tested using partial least squares structural equation modeling (PLS-SEM) with 5,000 bootstrap resamples. The results show that both POS_ATT (β = 0.312, p < 0.001) and RAIS (β = 0.287, p < 0.001) are positively associated with employee engagement. ENG, in turn, is positively associated with all three dimensions of Green Well-being, with the strongest relationship observed for emotional well-being (β = 0.441), followed by cognitive (β = 0.418) and social well-being (β = 0.397), all at p < 0.001. Moreover, ENG fully mediates the relationships between POS_ATT and RAIS and the three Green Well-being dimensions. These findings broaden understanding of sustainable development in AI-enabled workplaces by showing that the potential human benefits of Generative AI are not associated solely with technology adoption. Rather, favorable employee perceptions and responsible implementation need to be translated into meaningful work engagement before they are associated with sustainable well-being outcomes. The study therefore identifies responsible AI, employee engagement, and multidimensional well-being as interconnected elements of a human-centered approach to sustainable digital transformation. Practically, organizations should complement investments in AI capabilities with transparent, explainable, and fair AI governance and engagement-oriented work design to preserve and develop human resources during digital transformation. Because the cross-sectional design captures relationships at a single point in time, the findings establish associations rather than causal effects. Longitudinal and cross-national research is therefore needed to examine whether these relationships persist over time and contribute to long-term employee and organizational resilience. Keywords: Generative artificial intelligence; responsible AI; employee engagement; Green Well-being; sustainable development; sustainable digital transformation.

This research on study of students' motivation learning in Law using a process approach of 1st year in Faculty of Food Science, Savannakhet University, during the 2024-2025 academic year. Including 31 participants, 10 females (representing majors in Agribusiness and Marketing, Food Processing Technology, and Rural Development and Business Promotion) were selected via purposive sampling. The research instruments included lesson plans, pre-tests and post-tests, and a behavioral observation scale covering five dimensions: collaborative planning in group work, mutual assistance among members, enthusiasm and accuracy in data research, group and individual responsibility, and clarity and engagement in presentations. The research followed a one-group pre-test/post-test experimental design. Statistical analysis was conducted using percentages (%), mean (), standard deviation (S.D.), and the Dependent Sample t-test. The findings indicate that the learning outcomes for the Law course using the process approach method were significantly higher in the post-test than the pre-test, with a post-test mean score of () = 7.77 (S.D = 1.54) at a statistical significance level of 0.01. Behavioral observations revealed that students actively participated in activities, demonstrated high responsibility in group tasks, and supported one another. Students showed increased interest and enthusiasm due to the opportunities for self-directed thinking. Regarding attitudes toward the process approach teaching method, the evaluation score was 3.92, categorized at a "Good" level. This method emphasizes teamwork, review and exchange, which aids students in achieving accurate long-term retention. Furthermore, the study on student motivation revealed that both intrinsic and extrinsic motivations were present; however, intrinsic motivation was more dominant, with an overall mean of 4.84 compared to 3.55 for extrinsic motivation. In conclusion, intrinsic motivation is the exceptional for students in Faculty of Food Science, Savannakhet University.

Commercial Weaponization of Prize Problems: Artificial intelligence companies have transformed the one-million-dollar Clay Millennium Prize Problems into multi-trillion-dollar marketing vehicles, using binary formal proofs to project absolute reliability ahead of enterprise sales cycles and initial public offerings. Mathematical Vaudeville: Corporate publicity campaigns repackage physically sterile stunts—such as contrived blow-up constructions in idealized three-dimensional Navier-Stokes equations—and choreographed preprints on Yang-Mills theory and the Riemann Hypothesis as historic breakthroughs, despite offering no practical value for real fluid turbulence or engineering. Closed Formal Cages vs. Brute-Force Search: AI laboratories target Millennium problems because they are finite games with fixed axioms, bounded inference rules, and automated pass/fail verification signals, making them tractable via massive parallel tree search and reinforcement learning. The Chasm with Fundamental Physics: Unlike solving a pre-stated puzzle inside an unchanging logical labyrinth, discovering new laws of nature requires dismantling flawed axioms, interpreting physical anomalies, and creating new mathematical structures anchored in conservation laws and experimental reality. Distortion of Scientific Priorities: Funneling capital and prestige toward mechanical benchmark clearance sidelines slow, foundational inquiry and confuses automated verification with genuine physical discovery.

documents.abstract: Universities increasingly ask students to verify AI-generated content and to reveal AI help, but there is little knowledge of how EFL students experience these demands. This explanatory sequential mixed methods study investigated a convenience sample of 60 undergraduate EFL students at a Pakistani university for perceived utility, verification confidence, effort, honesty and willingness to reveal, then interviewed ten students. Most students (71.7%) agreed that verification helped them to take responsibility for accuracy but only 45.0% agreed that disclosure made writing more transparent, and that the willingness to make it public was the lowest for heavily revised text (42.4%). The willingness to disclose was the most associated with perceived fairness (ρ = .58). The perceived confidence in effort and verification was higher among frequent AI users and advanced students and only 45.0% of students reported receiving guidance on disclosure. Interview notes pointed to concerns about the quality and currency of AI-generated writing, fear about reduced brands as AI usage is announced, and a need for institutional guidance. Clear rules, practical disclosure examples, and training in checking references may make these demands fairer. Findings are exploratory, self-reported and context-specific, and two scales were in a low degree of reliability. Keywords: generative AI; EFL writing; AI disclosure; verification; academic integrity; writing assessment; student perceptions; Pakistan

An undergraduate can rehearse raising a missed deadline with a chatbot and still struggle when a teammate gives an unexpected explanation. This focused narrative review examines nine empirical studies according to the role of artificial intelligence (AI), the outcome assessed, and whether AI was available during assessment. The evidence most directly relevant to undergraduate team conflict documents strategies used during chatbot rehearsal and students’ reported confidence after instruction and practice. Studies in adjacent settings illustrate how to assess unaided performance with a human partner. Controlled studies in clinical settings show mixed results for the added benefit of AI practice. The reviewed evidence leaves open whether undergraduate students use the targeted behaviors in ordinary team interactions after AI rehearsal. A proposed classroom exercise combines AI rehearsal, behavior-based feedback, and unaided peer conversations. It distinguishes immediate application to a new scenario, delayed retention, and observation in actual teamwork. A proposed research design compares AI rehearsal with an equivalent amount of peer rehearsal.

documents.abstract: Background: This review examines when humanlike artificial intelligence (AI) becomes unsettling and how uncanny appraisal relates to consumer trust in AI-mediated brand communication. It integrates the trust-building logic of anthropomorphism with evidence of unfavorable trust-related evaluations under uncanny conditions. Methods: Following PRISMA 2020 and SPAR-4-SLR principles, a Scopus search identified 7,665 records. After duplicate, document-type, and title/abstract screening, 18 journal articles were retained, verified in full text, and coded by AI form, appraisal mechanism, trust object, boundary condition, outcome, and evidence directness. Additional theoretical sources were used for conceptual anchoring but were not added to the systematic evidence corpus. Results: Five studies provide direct uncanny-appraisal evidence, six proximal-appraisal evidence, and seven contextual anthropomorphism–trust evidence. Direct studies associate unfavorable uncanny appraisal with lower trust-related evaluation, using distinct measures of affect, trust, and source trustworthiness. Human-likeness is not inherently harmful: social cues can support trust when aligned with competence, empathy, usefulness, transparency, and task demands. Conclusion: The review develops the Eeriness-Trust Calibration Framework (ETCF), separating design cues from consumer appraisals, positive and negative trust routes, and multiple trust objects. It reframes AI humanization as a cue-capability-context calibration problem and identifies cross-object trust transfer to organizations and brands as a key unresolved marketing mechanism. Brands should optimize coherence rather than maximize realism, pretest eeriness and authenticity together, and monitor trust separately at agent, content, provider, and brand levels.
topics: Consumer Behavior in Brand Consumption and Identification

documents.abstract: Generative artificial intelligence intervenes in the domain of imagination by making images, narratives, and possible worlds immediately available, often preceding the learner’s own exploration and elaboration. Drawing on theoretical analysis and empirical evidence, this paper brings Munari’s distinction among fantasy, invention, creativity, and imagination into dialogue with sociocultural approaches and theories of material engagement. It conceptualises artificial imagination as a transformation of the symbolic and material environment in which human imaginative activity unfolds, without attributing imagination, in the human sense, to AI systems. Techno-material plasticity describes the twofold influence of technological devices: they shape the conditions of generation and enable subsequent transformations of generated forms. Research on learning, engagement, and creativity indicates educational potential alongside risks of fixation, homogenisation, and delegation. On this basis, the paper outlines a pedagogy of engagement centred on learners’ interpretive agency: autonomous elaboration before generation, critical examination of errors and impossibilities, manipulation and recomposition of outputs, and reflective documentation of processes. The educational value of generation depends on treating outputs as material for further elaboration while preserving the time required for experience, judgement, and learner authorship.

Poor workplace ergonomics is a growing yet under-investigated occupational health concern in Pakistan’s expanding corporate sector. This study estimated the prevalence of self-reported musculoskeletal symptoms; described perceived workplace ergonomic conditions and sedentary behaviour among desk-based employees in Islamabad; examined their correlates; and documented organisational ergonomic practices as reported by human resources (HR) officers. A cross-sectional survey with an embedded qualitative (free-text) component was conducted in Islamabad between 2024 and 2025 among a purposive sample of 251 respondents: 179 desk-based office employees and 72 HR officers. Employees and HR officers were recruited independently and could not be linked to one another at the organisational level, so the two strands are reported as complementary perspectives and never as a paired organisational comparison. Two distinct instruments were used. The employee instrument, informed by the item content of the Cornell Musculoskeletal Discomfort Questionnaire (CMDQ) and the Rapid Office Strain Assessment (ROSA) checklist, captured self-reported symptoms, workstation characteristics and sedentary patterns; neither tool was administered as a scored assessment. The HR instrument captured organisation-level ergonomic policy and practice. The two instruments shared no items in common, so the two groups are reported separately and not pooled. Qualitative data came from open-ended items embedded in the employee survey; we conducted no in-depth interviews. Analyses in SPSS version 21 comprised frequencies with 95% confidence intervals, chi-square tests and multivariable logistic regression. We conducted inductive thematic analysis of open-ended responses, integrating themes through a joint display. Associations are cross-sectional and are reported as adjusted odds ratios; they describe associations, not prediction or causation. Among the 179 employees, 124 (69.3%) had never received ergonomic training, although 156 (87.2%) believed ergonomic improvement would reduce workplace fatigue. An adjustable chair supporting the back was available to 106 (59.2%) and a screen at eye level to 120 (67.0%). At least one musculoskeletal symptom was reported by 127 (70.9%, 95% CI 64.3–77.6), and 102 (57.0%) reported symptoms at two or more body sites. Back pain was the most prevalent single symptom (100, 55.9%), followed by shoulder discomfort (98, 54.7%), eye strain or headaches (92, 51.4%), neck discomfort (90, 50.3%) and wrist pain (70, 39.1%). Persistent pain developing over time was reported by 84 (46.9%), and 62 (34.6%) had sought medical treatment. Sixty-eight employees (38.0%) sat for seven hours or more daily, and 53 (29.6%) rarely took movement breaks. A screen positioned at eye level was independently associated with lower odds of neck discomfort (adjusted OR 0.32, 95% CI 0.15–0.70), shoulder discomfort (0.33, 95% CI 0.15–0.73), and back pain (0.32, 95% CI 0.15–0.69). Female employees reported substantially higher symptom prevalence than male employees at every site (any symptom 86.6% versus 61.6%; adjusted OR for male sex 0.22, 95% CI 0.09–0.53). Among HR officers, 44 (61.1%) reported a formal ergonomics policy; only 24 (33.3%) reported that their organisation provided ergonomic training; 25 (34.7%) tracked discomfort reports; and 44 (61.1%) allocated under 5% of the budget to ergonomic improvements. Thematic analysis identified five organisational barriers: budgetary constraints, managerial knowledge gaps, organisational inertia, spatial limitations and reluctance to raise complaints. Self-reported musculoskeletal symptoms were common among desk-based employees in this Islamabad sample, and basic ergonomic provisions and training were frequently absent. Screen height was the workstation characteristic most consistently associated with symptoms, and female employees carried a markedly higher symptom burden. HR officers commonly reported formal ergonomic policies, while employees commonly reported a lack of training and monitoring; because the two respondent groups were not linked at the organisational level, these are complementary perspectives on ergonomic provision and do not demonstrate organisation-level discordance. Workstation review, ergonomic training and accessible reporting channels are plausible low-cost priorities; prospective and intervention studies are required to establish causation and effectiveness.
topics: Occupational Health and Safety in Workplaces

documents.abstract: Computational Thinking (CT) develops critical thinking and problem-solving skills in learners systematically. Modern AI tutors can help learners solve problems effectively; however, they generate direct answers and mostly fail to integrate the pedagogical principles focused on CT components to improve students’ problem-solving skills. This failure raises concern in the development of CT skills for early learners. Our project, ProgCT is a pedagogy-grounded multi-agent tutor that helps learners develop computational problem-solving abilities through CT practices. As learners work through each problem, the agents (i) assess the CT skills learners demonstrate, (ii) analyze learners’ cognitive engagement, and (iii) guide learners through the relevant CT steps with Socratic hints without revealing the solution. In a pretest post-test study on Python programming concepts involving seven learners (n=7), the mean score of the Algorithmic Thinking Test for Adults (ATTA) rose from 64.8% to 77.6%, and self-assessed confidence on the Hi-ACT test increased in all six CT components – abstraction, decomposition, pattern recognition, algorithm design, evaluation and generalization. The system’s built-in progress evaluation module also recorded increases in participants’ CT ownership and cognitive engagement on later exercises compared with earlier exercises of the same difficulty.

The rapid Digitalization of organizational work, accelerated by Artificial Intelligence, hybrid work, ubiquitous connectivity, and continuous information exchange, has created unprece dented opportunities for productivity. Simultaneously the issues of intensifying digital overload, cognitive fatigue, work interruptions, technostress, and emotional exhaustion have been non-trivial challenges for organizations. Existing organizational stress-management approaches predominantly emphasize individual coping or post-stress interventions and provide limited integration of real-time Digital Stress detection, adaptive regulation, responsible technology governance, and sustainable productivity. Addressing the above challenges and the research gap, we propose a Digital Stress Resilience Model grounded in Sustainable Positive Computing, Self-awareness, Affective Computing, Organizational Psychology, and Responsible Artificial intelligence. Our proposed model conceptualizes Digital Stress Management as a continuous socio-technical process comprising five interconnected capabilities such as Digital Stress Perception, Cognitive-Emotional Intelligence, Adaptive Stress Regulation, Responsible Digital Governance, and Resilience-Oriented Productivity Management. The model provides a conceptual roadmap for transforming organizations from reactive stress-management environments into proactive, self-aware, resilient, responsible, and productive digital workplaces. A mixed-method research design is proposed for subsequent empirical validation using digital workload, cognitive load, emotional regulation, resilience, responsible technology use, employee engagement, and sustainable productivity indicators.

Effective collaboration between humans and artificial intelligence (AI) in industry 5.0 demands technological systems with human social-cognitive processes, such as trust calibration and shared mental model. This study introduces human-centric decision-making framework for configuring human-AI collaboration in smart manufacturing systems. As Industry 5.0 evolves, finding the best synergy between human intelligence and collaborative robots (cobots) becomes crucial for enhancing adaptability, safety, efficiency, and sustainability. The proposed methodology uses neutrosophic Z-numbers (NZN) to capture uncertainty with three components: truth, indeterminacy, and falsity with their associated reliabilities, and the NZN weighted arithmetic averaging (NZNWAA) operator to combine individual preferences of decision-makers. Afterward, the criteria importance through intercriteria correlation (CRITIC) method is used to objectively determine the importance of each criterion by analyzing contrast intensity and inter-criteria correlation. The ranking of alternatives is then obtained using the compromise ranking of alternatives from distance to ideal solution (CRADIS) method. This hybrid NZN-CRITIC-CRADIS approach is applied to a real-world case study of BMW manufacturing systems, assessing four human-AI collaboration strategies: full AI automation, partial cobot integration, human-led AI-assisted assembly, and hybrid multi-agent collaboration, across four critical criteria. The results of the study show that the AI-assisted assembly emerges as the most suitable solution, balancing technological capability with human-centric design. The effectiveness of the proposed approach has been further validated through a sensitivity analysis and a comparative assessment with existing decision-making techniques, where our model consistently demonstrated superior performance in handling uncertainty and maintaining objectivity. Ultimately, this study offers a reliable human-centered framework that emphasizes socially intelligent manufacturing.

documents.abstract: Ambient artificial intelligence (AI) scribes are being adopted to reduce clinical documentation burden, but evidence from the emergency department (ED), a high-acuity, frequently interrupted setting, remains limited. We evaluated ED clinicians’ perceptions of an ambient AI documentation platform (Ambience) implemented across two EDs in one United States health system, using a two-round cross-sectional survey and inductive qualitative content analysis of free-text responses. Twenty-three clinicians provided 34 responses. All responses (100%) reported high overall satisfaction and enhanced focus during patient encounters, and all rated willingness to recommend the platform 4 or 5 on a 1-to-5 scale; enhanced documentation quality and improved work-life balance were each reported in 32 of 34 responses (94%). Among 18 responses from clinicians with prior human-scribe experience, 16 (89%) used a human scribe and Ambience together rather than as substitutes, and views on whether Ambience alone would be as efficient were divided. Content analysis identified documentation efficiency (21/34) and note detail capture (21/34) as the most emphasized strengths, with accuracy limitations (10/34) and workflow friction (6/34) as recurring concerns. Restricting analysis to first submissions ( n = 23) did not change the pattern. Findings are favorable but limited by small size, repeated responses, and positively framed items.

documents.abstract: This study explores the general understandings of mindfulness and applies Self-Determination Theory (SDT) to examine perceived competence, relatedness, and autonomy in practicing mindfulness among Promotora/es de Salud (PdS) in Colorado. Twenty-one PdS (two male, nineteen female) participated in semi-structured qualitative interviews about their knowledge, experiences, and perceptions of mindfulness. Thematic analysis combined inductive and deductive approaches, analyzing motivational themes using SDT constructs, where applicable. PdS initially associated mindfulness with “slowing down” and “self-care” but were often unfamiliar with the formal term or its origin. After receiving a standardized definition, many recognized these as practices they already used without formal labeling. Exposure to mindfulness was primarily linked to professional workshops or therapy. In the SDT-informed questions, participants commonly preferred guided or hybrid options, foundational training such as instructional videos and structured feedback, and group-based over independent sessions. These preferences were interpreted in relation to autonomy, competence, and relatedness, without knowing if the study measured intrinsic motivation or need satisfaction. Most PdS were open to spiritual or religious references, though some preferred secular or flexible framing. Concepts consistent with mindfulness were familiar and acceptable to many PdS and were already reflected in descriptions of self-care. The SDT-informed findings identified preferences for choice in practice format, skill-building supports, and social connection. These findings offer formative considerations for future culturally and contextually responsive well-being programming rather than evidence of intervention effectiveness. These findings provide preliminary guidance for designing and testing future mindfulness interventions with PdS, including flexible practice options, foundational education and feedback, and opportunities for group-based practice.

documents.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are being increasingly integrated into immersive environments and design workflows, providing application prospects in areas such as rapid scene prototyping for non-expert users and scene understanding capabilities for accessibility design. While many workflows that incorporate LLMs in immersive spaces are proposed, such systems can exhibit errors, potentially resulting in frustration, loss of user trust, and compromised user safety. This paper studies the underexplored area of LLM confabulations in immersive 3D scene editing contexts. Through an exploratory study with 24 non-expert users, we construct a taxonomy of the different types of confabulation observed in LLM-assisted immersive 3D scene editing. We report their prevalence and perceived disruptiveness, and define the construct perception-reality gap to help understand the gap between the actual and perceived occurrence of confabulations. We highlight the observed saturation of confabulation awareness under load and conclude by discussing design implications for confabulation mitigation in future LLM-assisted systems in immersive 3D scenes.

Oral communication skills remain critical for the workplace at a time of significant technological disruption. While anecdotal evidence suggests workers are using AI to develop these skills through methods such as role-play and feedback, there is a lack of empirical data on how widespread this usage is. This study surveyed working adults in Aotearoa New Zealand (N = 478) on their use of AI to build oral communication skills. Findings show 26.2% had used AI for this purpose in the past six months, just behind the two most common non-AI methods. Where respondents named an AI tool they had used, these were almost all general-purpose tools such as ChatGPT or Copilot, instead of specialised AI communication tools. Usage was predominantly text-based rather than voice-based and centred more on preparation than on practice or reflection. This suggests a potential gap between assistance and skill development, with AI used more to prepare what to say than to practise how to say it or strengthen the underlying skills.

During mass casualty incidents in crowded places, ordinary civilians can play a critical role in saving lives and mitigating harm before professional responders arrive. Yet remarkably little empirical evidence exists regarding public attitudes towards active bystander intervention, individuals’ willingness to intervene, and the factors shaping that willingness. This study addresses this gap through a survey of 1219 Australian adults. Aggregate analyses were complemented by a series of econometric models to identify the demographic, experiential, and psychosocial characteristics associated with attitudes towards intervention and willingness to act. Previous exposure to mass emergency events emerged as the strongest and most consistent predictor of favourable attitudes towards intervention, as well as intervention propensity. Emergency training and professional preparedness were also associated with stronger intervention propensity, reduced reliance on social proof, and lower sensitivity to personal risk. Men consistently reported greater willingness to intervene and greater acceptance of personal risk. Self-reported spirituality (but not religiosity) was positively associated with intervention propensity. Australians appear to hold a nuanced normative position in which active bystander intervention is regarded simultaneously as a societal value and a matter of personal choice rather than moral obligation. Public attitudes towards self-sacrificial intervention were nevertheless polarised, with one (larger) group rejecting any moral duty to intervene and another (smaller, though sizable) group considering the prospect of saving even a single life sufficient to create a moral obligation to act. The study offers an empirical foundation for informing public preparedness initiatives, immediate responder programmes, and policy development, as well as future research aimed at understanding how societies can better harness the capacity of ordinary civilians to save lives and mitigate harm during mass casualty events. Future cross-national comparisons remain necessary to identify cultural differences in attitudes towards civilian intervention.

Extended Reality (XR) headsets increasingly host familiar 2D user interfaces as windows floating in physical environments. However, their usability depends on environmental conditions that designers cannot fully control. Current design workflows often separate how a variant is designed from how it actually looks in the target environment. We present AdapTest , an in-situ authoring and testing tool that lets designers select interface elements, define when and how they change, compare the resulting variations, and test their activation without coding. Based on prior research and a formative study with 12 interface designers, the system targets three key environmental variables: distance, lighting, and occlusion. We evaluated AdapTest against a desktop design and in-headset preview workflow in a within-subjects study with 12 designers. Compared with the baseline, designers accounted for a wider range of environmental factors, addressed more overlapping conditions, and repeatedly tested and revised their designs in place; there were no significant differences in workload or usability despite longer sessions. Our work contributes an integrated, designer-centered approach to adapting, comparing, and validating environmentally responsive XR user interfaces.

Online safety is a pressing concern, yet its harms fall unevenly, particularly on communities whose needs mainstream safety tools were not designed to meet, such as women and gender-diverse people, LGBTQ+ communities, culturally and linguistically diverse communities, and people with disability. At the same time, artificial intelligence is reshaping this landscape as both a source of new harms and a proposed remedy. These challenges are hard to address because online safety research remains fragmented across HCI sub-fields and adjacent disciplines, with limited communication between them. This workshop brings together researchers, designers, policymakers, industry practitioners, and community advocates, from within and beyond HCI, to examine two questions: which groups are most vulnerable to online harms and need greater attention, and in what ways does AI enhance online safety or create and intensify online risks? Through structured discussion and collaborative activities organised around case studies and scenarios of exclusion, participants will identify communities that need greater attention, interrogate the dual role of AI, and build interdisciplinary networks and a shared research agenda, advancing collaborative research directions within Australia and beyond toward more inclusive and effective responses to online safety.

documents.abstract: The rapid development of agentic artificial intelligence introduces a challenge that extends beyond the control of individual AI agents.Multiple agents, each operating within an individually defined operational perimeter, mayinteract in ways that produce collective behaviour. Such behaviour may include recurringinteraction patterns, the propagation of objectives, shared strategies and coordinatedoperations. In some circumstances, collective coordination may emerge without an explicit instruction to coordinate. This raises an important architectural question:Can a collection of individually controlled agents develop collective behaviour thatexceeds the operational perimeter defined by humans? The ST-T1024 A17 proposal addresses this question as a complementary researchextension to the existing A1–A16 architecture. Its initial design proposes a Spiking Neural Network (SNN) for temporal pattern learning and detection, a Learning Set (LS) containing previously identified swarm sequences, and acontinuously updated memory mechanism (MEMO) for observing current and past agentactivity. The central research hypothesis is that coordination may produce what this paper calls Enhanced Repetitions: recurring patterns that are reinforced, extended and propagatedthrough interactions among agents. A17 proposes a Boolean detection output:● SWARM = 1: identify the participating agents as a detected collective operation andprevent them from continuing that coordinated operation.● SWARM = 0: continue observing and memorizing the sequences. The proposal does not assume that coordination is necessarily malicious. Detecting collective behaviour, determining whether it exceeds human authorization, and determining whether it is harmful are separate questions. A17 is presented as an open research and architectural proposal. Its algorithms, learningmethodology, memory parameters, detection performance and implementation remainsubjects for independent investigation and experimental validation. The governing principle is simple: humans define the operational perimeter; agentsoperate within it; collective agency must not redefine it.

documents.abstract: Generative artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly embedded in health and care for clinical support and to mediate collaboration within design processes. While co-design is well established in health and care, how generative AI-driven tools influence inclusivity, participation, sense-making and power dynamics remains underexplored. Our research explored the role of generative AI in co-design activities in high-stakes health and care settings. We report findings from an HCI conference workshop involving ten researchers and practitioners engaged in health and care intervention design. Activities were structured using the Double Diamond Framework supported by four generative AI tools. Our findings showed key roles specific generative AI tools can play across the different stages of the design process. However, participants identified challenges that may introduce bias and constrain co-design practice. The findings highlighted that strong human mediation is essential for effective AI-assisted co-design enabling reflective, inclusive and responsible design practice in health and care.

Artificial Intelligence (AI)-powered voice technologies have emerged as valuable tools in enhancing crisis communication during pandemics and disasters, yet their use in the United States (U.S.) remains fragmented. This scoping review identified and mapped evidence on AI-enabled voice intelligence for pandemic and disaster response in the U.S. and developed an evidence-informed National Voice Intelligence Emergency Preparedness Framework (NVIEPF). The review was carried out based on the Joanna Briggs Institute methodology and PRISMA-ScR reporting guidance. The literature was searched from key bibliographic databases and grey literature sources between January 2015 and May 2026. Fifteen eligible records were synthesized using evidence mapping and thematic analysis. Current applications were primarily limited to speech recognition, automatic transcription, conversational agents, multilingual communication, and decision support in public safety communication systems. The biggest challenges were the lack of a unified communication system, the lack of consistency in implementation, limited interoperability, governance issues, cybersecurity issues, and the lack of proper evaluation in operational contexts. This research contributed to the conceptualization of the NVIEPF, which has five interconnected components that involve AI-based early warning, crisis communication, surveillance, resource coordination, and community feedback, all with human oversight. The evidence was limited by its reliance on programme reports, observational studies, and operational documentation, with limited evaluation in real-world emergency settings. Although evidence of widespread adoption of AI-driven voice technologies is limited, the framework provides a means for future research, policy development, and a phased approach to integrating AI-powered voice intelligence into the national preparedness system in the U.S.

documents.abstract: Existing research has demonstrated the benefits and envisioned broader applications of using extended reality (XR) head-mounted displays (HMDs) to create virtual display extensions for personal computers (PCs), offering a more flexible and cost-effective alternative to traditional physical monitors. This combined setup, with inputs from both sources available, provides users with more options for interaction. In this work, we aim to understand the advantages and disadvantages of these inputs and their interaction techniques in the fundamental window placement tasks in virtual displays enabled by the combined use of a PC and an HMD. With their standard inputs, we identified five potential hand-based window placement techniques: Mouse Cursor, Pinch Drag, Keyboard Shortcut, Touchpad Gesture, and Wrist Bending. We conducted a mixed-design user study (N = 40) to evaluate user performance and experience with these window placement techniques in two display setups: a fully virtual setup where the HMD displays all windows, and a hybrid setup involving a laptop screen in addition to the HMD’s virtual windows. All five techniques were evaluated in a structured layout task, while Mouse Cursor and Pinch Drag were additionally compared in a freeform placement task. Across both setups, Mouse Cursor was faster than Pinch Drag, while Keyboard Shortcut and Touchpad Gesture were faster and produced fewer failed trials than Wrist Bending. Laptop-based techniques also received higher usability ratings and lower perceived workload ratings than mid-air techniques. Nevertheless, some participants preferred mid-air techniques, valuing their naturalness. Our empirical findings can guide the future design of cross-device and cross-reality interactions between XR HMDs and PCs.

Purpose: This study examined the effects of learning motivation, behavioral engagement, cognitive engagement, emotional engagement, agentic engagement, and feedback on college students’ learning performance in physical education. Research design, data and methodology: This study adopted a mixed-methods action research design. The questionnaire was developed based on established literature, and content validity was assessed using the Index of Item-Objective Congruence. Reliability was confirmed through a pilot test with 30 students using Cronbach’s alpha. Quantitative data were collected from 169 valid questionnaires administered to undergraduate students at Guizhou University and analyzed using multiple linear regression to examine relationships between the variables. Based on the regression results and qualitative insights from student interviews, an eight-week Intervention Design Implementation was conducted with 30 students. Paired-sample t-tests were used to compare pre-intervention and post-intervention results. Results: The multiple linear regression analysis indicated that emotional engagement (β = 0.437) and feedback (β = 0.572) had significant positive effects on learning performance, while the other variables showed no significant direct effects. The paired-sample t-test results revealed significant improvements across all variables, including learning performance, after the intervention. Conclusions: The findings suggest that integrating emotional engagement, feedback, and supportive intervention activities can effectively enhance learning performance and support the development of sustained physical exercise habits among college students.

Digital transformation requires employees to develop digital technical competence and understand the use and limitations of artificial intelligence (AI) in their work. This study examines the roles of digital technical competence and AI literacy in supporting asset management at PT Lancar Wiguna Sejahtera (Lawson), a retail company. A qualitative case study approach was employed, with data collected through interviews involving five informants representing asset administration, store operations, information technology, area supervision, and maintenance functions. The findings indicate that digital technical competence supports the use of internal applications, asset recording, reporting, information verification, and asset status updates. However, the asset management process still faces challenges related to incomplete information, delayed reporting, discrepancies between administrative records and actual asset conditions, and limited visibility of follow-up status. AI literacy involves understanding AI capabilities and limitations, evaluating AI-generated outputs, and protecting confidential company information. The interviews indicate that AI is considered a potential tool for summarizing reports and organizing information, but its outputs require verification against official company records, field conditions, technical knowledge, and operational procedures. No evidence was found that AI had been integrated into the company's official asset management system or used for predictive maintenance. The study highlights the importance of task-based training, mentoring, standardized reporting procedures, information security awareness, and coordination among organizational roles to support more effective asset management.

Artificial intelligence (AI) is reshaping the field of analytics, understood as the continuum from descriptive business intelligence to predictive and prescriptive analytics augmented by machine learning. While organizations are acquiring these systems on a massive scale, the persistent gap between equipment rates and actual usage rates remains largely unexplained. The frameworks inherited from information systems adoption research (the technology acceptance model, the unified theory of acceptance and use of technology, the technology-organization-environment framework, and the diffusion of innovations) were built for systems governed by explicit and auditable rules; their relevance to opaque, partially agentic, and ethically problematic systems has not been systematically examined. This article maps the factors of analytics adoption in the age of AI. The corpus derives from a scoping review that was reported following the PRISMA-ScR protocol: 16,113 records identified, 11,170 screened, 1097 assessed for eligibility, and 42 articles analyzed. The corpus was processed through inductive qualitative content analysis following the Gioia methodology. Coding yielded 106 first-order concepts, 18 s-order themes, and 6 aggregate dimensions. The reliability of the categorization was checked through independent double coding of 18.9% of the coding units: raw agreement reached 80.0%, and Cohen’s kappa was 0.79. The most frequently discussed factors are not the performance attributes of the technology but the socio-organizational and epistemic conditions of its appropriation. The article proposes a moderated mediation model built on three layers: the enabling layer occupies the position of antecedent; the legitimating layer, specific to the age of AI, that of mediator and bottleneck of adoption; and the two dimensions of the actualizing layer that of moderators.

documents.abstract: Why do female leaders face professional penalties for the same expressions of anger that often benefit male leaders? Despite decades of research, gender bias in leadership evaluations remains a stubborn hurdle for women seeking career advancement. In this theoretical paper, I develop a stereotype-context competition model to explain how gender bias arises in the evaluation of leaders who express anger, and to identify conditions under which such bias is less likely to occur. I argue that evaluations of angry leaders are shaped by two competing forces: a pro-bias force driven by stereotype information and a counter-bias force driven by contextual information. I further propose that the pro-bias force generally prevails, resulting in the persistence of gender bias in initial evaluations of angry leaders. Finally, I identify three categories of factors—related to the leader, the observer, and the situation—that can reduce the likelihood of gender bias. I conclude by discussing the theoretical and practical implications of the model.

When a viewer reports that they trust a visualization, what have we measured? Trust measurement in visualization has improved: validated multidimensional inventories are replacing single-item ratings. This position paper argues that level measures answer only part of the question that matters for design. They record how much a person trusts, not whether that trust is warranted or how it changes with use. Research on trust in automation and AI-assisted decision making has long treated calibration, the fit between trust and trustworthiness, as the target. We ask whether that agenda shapes how visualization studies measure trust. Auditing sixteen recent journal studies, six from visualization and ten from an adjacent services literature, we find three gaps. The construct is fragmented. Where visualization experiments record what trust could be judged against, they use different referents and rarely analyse trust against them; the services studies record none. And no design follows trust through failure and repair. We argue that calibration should supplement level measures, identify what trust in a visualization can be calibrated against, and specify the metrics and designs this requires.

This record contains a complete, ready-to-deliver half-day training package on the practical and responsible use of Artificial Intelligence (AI) in medical research, developed for clinicians and researchers at Ayder Comprehensive Specialized Hospital, Mekelle University. The 32-slide presentation, scheduled from 08:30 to 12:30 with a coffee break, guides participants through the research lifecycle in seven sessions covering AI foundations and prompting, literature searching and study design, academic writing and publishing, qualitative and quantitative data analysis, and ethics, privacy, and verification. Each stage includes realistic, ready-to-use prompt examples for tools such as ChatGPT, PubMed, Google Scholar, and Elicit, alongside live demonstrations of AI-assisted statistical analysis using Stata and R. No technical background is assumed. All acronyms, including AI, ML, LLM, NLP, RAG, PICO/PICOT, PRISMA, and ICMJE, are spelled out and explained in plain language. Relevant research reporting standards, including STROBE, CONSORT, PRISMA, CARE, and EQUATOR, are also introduced at the appropriate stages. To encourage active participation, the training incorporates three hands-on activities: identifying fabricated references, improving an academic abstract, and completing a 20-minute research sprint. The presentation concludes with a two-slide glossary and a verified reference list. Every slide includes detailed, structured speaker notes covering the opening, explanation, practical example, key message, transition, and presenter guidance. This enables any facilitator, including those without a medical or informatics background, to deliver the training confidently. A companion trainer's workbook is also included in this record, containing the training run sheet, timed talking points, demonstration runbooks, activity answer keys, a question-and-answer bank, and a pronunciation guide. All scenarios, quotations, and datasets used throughout the training are fictional or synthetic, ensuring that no real patient information is used. The training consistently emphasises the importance of human oversight and responsible AI use: AI provides drafts and assistance; researchers remain responsible for decisions, verification, and final outputs.

documents.abstract: Heart failure affects more than 64 million people worldwide and remains associated with high mortality and recurrent hospitalisation. Artificial intelligence (AI), including large language models (LLMs), is being evaluated across the care pathway, but evidence maturity varies by task. The aim of this narrative review was to appraise direct evidence for LLM applications in heart failure, distinguish it from supporting evidence for other AI methods and propose a risk-based framework for clinical evaluation and governance. The strongest direct LLM evidence concerns electronic health record extraction, document drafting, patient information and clinical trial endpoint adjudication. A small, randomised pilot evaluated supervised generative-AI-guided optimisation of guideline-directed medical therapy. Prospective case-finding and monitoring evidence largely concerns non-LLM AI. For conversational AI telemonitoring (a natural language interface with rule-based alerting), prospective evidence was limited to a single non-randomised controlled pilot. Performance depends on task definition, data completeness, human review and workflow adoption. Overall, LLMs can support clearly defined, supervised heart failure tasks, but current evidence does not justify autonomous high-stakes care. The evidence base is expanding but predominantly retrospective. Prospective trials, disease-specific benchmarks, equity assessment and regulatory engagement are prerequisites for safe clinical translation. Human oversight remains essential across all current-generation applications.

documents.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) has rapidly emerged as a promising resource for supporting students with dyslexia. Nevertheless, much of the existing literature examines AI primarily as an assistive technology, with limited attention to the cognitive mechanisms through which it may enhance reading development. This paper addresses that gap by proposing a conceptual framework that integrates Baddeley’s multicomponent model of working memory with contemporary AI-supported educational tools. Drawing on research in cognitive psychology, special education, cognitive load theory, Universal Design for Learning (UDL), and self-determination theory, the paper argues that AI should be understood not merely as an instructional aid but as an external cognitive support system that complements and extends the functional capacity of working memory during reading. Specifically, the framework illustrates how AI technologies—including text-to-speech systems, speech recognition, adaptive learning environments, and generative AI applications—may reduce cognitive load while supporting the phonological loop, visuospatial sketchpad, central executive, and episodic buffer. Through this cognitive alignment, AI has the potential to facilitate decoding, comprehension, learner engagement, and reading autonomy among students with dyslexia. The proposed framework contributes to the literature by offering a theoretically grounded perspective that connects cognitive theory with emerging educational technologies. Rather than evaluating the effectiveness of a specific intervention, the paper provides an integrative model to guide future empirical research, instructional design, and the development of AI-supported reading interventions for learners with dyslexia.

Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly used in career guidance, occupational recommendation, and candidate-job matching, yet these applications are often treated as interchangeable despite serving different stakeholders and creating distinct downstream risks. This structured methodological review examines how AI methods are evaluated across career matching and algorithmic trustworthiness. Two semantic searches identified 980 unique records, of which 181 studies published in 2020–2026 met the extraction criteria under screening. We purposively selected 19 primary studies for in-depth analysis. Although the field has grown rapidly (62.4% of candidate studies appeared in 2025–2026), the close-read studies show that model performance depends heavily on proxy labels and validation design. High offline performance (area under the curve (AUC) > 0.92) did not consistently translate into robust outcomes: performance degraded for job seekers with few recorded work experiences, a graph baseline reached an AUC of only 0.641, and multimodal interview scoring added negligible predictive gain over text (Spearman ρ = 0.46 vs 0.45) while visual features showed adverse impact (ratio: 0.52). The advantage of fair re-ranking narrowed as employers made more selections, and screeners conformed more often to incorrect recommendations from a bag-of-words model than from a neural model. These findings demonstrate the limitations of static offline metrics. We propose a four-level evaluation framework addressing representation validity, decision-stage stress-testing, human-AI interaction, and consequential impact. Because retrieval was incomplete and inclusion decisions were not independently re-adjudicated, this review assesses methodological practices rather than claiming an exhaustive census.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is incorporated into frameworks for teaching, learning, assessment, and educational organization. This critical integrative review examines how these frameworks accommodate AI and the evidence associated with their use. The review used purposive web searches and included publications available by mid-October 2026. The synthesis distinguishes application, contextual specification, construct extension, relational reconfiguration, and AI-specific synthesis across professional knowledge, curriculum, learning, design, inclusion, assessment, and adoption. A source-to-entry crosswalk documents 120 analytical entries linked to 123 publications. Thirty empirical reports and one design case receive a structured access and appraisal record. All 31 selected records were examined in full text. Framework classifications based on partial material remain provisional. The comparison identifies tensions concerning ethical judgment, allocation of cognitive work, and attribution of understanding. Reported competence, AI-assisted products, and independent performance support different educational claims. A worked construct crosswalk shows how agency, regulation, and ethical judgment require distinct units and observations. Science, technology, engineering, and mathematics (STEM) provides disciplinary examples within a broader educational scope. The resulting research priorities connect proposed conceptual changes with the evidence needed to examine them.

documents.abstract: Artificial intelligence has become an influential factor in contemporary English language teaching because it expands access to feedback, practice, and personalised learning support. This article examines the role of artificial intelligence in English language teaching and analyses innovative learning approaches associated with its integration. The study is based on a qualitative review of recent academic and policy literature. The findings indicate that AI contributes most visibly to speaking practice, writing support, adaptive learning, learner autonomy, and classroom innovation. At the same time, the literature highlights important challenges, including ethical concerns, overreliance on technology, limited teacher preparation, and the need to preserve meaningful human interaction in the learning process. The article concludes that artificial intelligence should be used not as a replacement for the teacher, but as a pedagogical resource that becomes effective only when integrated critically, ethically, and methodologically.

The growing use of artificial intelligence (AI) in scientific research is changing how data are analysed, hypotheses are generated, and explanations are developed. Algorithmic systems increasingly participate in operations previously carried out directly by researchers. Their contribution, however, raises a methodological question: under what conditions can AI-generated outputs be regarded as justified scientific results rather than merely useful information? This paper examines the capabilities and limitations of AI in scientific inquiry, focusing on the distinction between statistical regularities and causal explanation, the validation of hypotheses, scientific understanding, reproducibility, and researchers' epistemic autonomy. The conceptual basis of this analysis is the distinction between participation in cognitive operations and independent epistemic subjecthood. In the extended-mind approach, external resources may become functionally integrated into human cognition. AI-assisted research likewise involves a distribution of cognitive operations between researchers and algorithmic systems.

documents.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is growing faster than ever and changing many parts of our lives. At the same time, emotional intelligence (EI) remains a key human skill that guides our decisions, relationships, and ethical choices. However, there is a growing tension between the strengths of AI and the unique abilities of EI. This article examines how AI and EI interact and sometimes clash, focusing on the balance between technological efficiency and human empathy. By analyzing examples from business, education, and everyday life, the article shows that neither AI nor EI alone can solve all problems. Instead, the future depends on combining the speed and logic of AI with the understanding and insight of EI. Understanding this balance is essential for creating a society that is both advanced and truly human-centered.

documents.abstract: This study examines how artificial intelligence-driven assessment systems shape examination integrity across Joint Admissions and Matriculation Board (JAMB) Computer-Based Test (CBT) centres in Nigeria. The study adopted a cross-sectional survey design and drew on a sample of 400 respondents comprising CBT centre supervisors, invigilators, technical officers and returning candidates, selected through multistage sampling across six geopolitical zones. Data were gathered with a structured questionnaire whose reliability returned a Cronbach's alpha of 0.87, and were analysed using descriptive statistics, Pearson correlation and multiple regression. The findings indicate that AI biometric authentication, AI-enabled remote proctoring and AI anomaly detection each exert a positive and statistically significant effect on examination integrity, with the combined model explaining roughly 61 per cent of the variance in integrity outcomes. Infrastructure reliability and invigilator digital literacy emerged as meaningful conditioning factors. The study concludes that AI systems have measurably strengthened the credibility of JAMB examinations, though their gains remain hostage to power supply, connectivity and human capacity. Recommendations centre on infrastructure investment, sustained capacity-building and a transparent governance framework for algorithmic decision-making in high-stakes assessment

Artificial intelligence (AI) has become increasingly integrated into modern justice systems, influencing decision-making in criminal justice, hiring, surveillance, healthcare, and public administration. Although AI promises efficiency and consistency, a growing body of research documents risks of algorithmic bias and unequal performance across demographic groups. This paper examines the relationship between artificial intelligence, gender bias, and human rights within contemporary justice systems through a qualitative, interdisciplinary analysis combining a narrative review of scholarly literature with doctrinal analysis of relevant international and European legal and ethical frameworks. It considers how biased datasets, discriminatory or uneven algorithmic outcomes, and unequal technological representation may affect fairness, equality, privacy, due process, and access to justice. Particular attention is given to documented evidence on facial-analysis systems and automated recruitment, while broader claims concerning institutional legitimacy and human-centered justice are treated as normative implications rather than empirical findings. The paper also evaluates regulatory responses, including Regulation (EU) 2024/1689 (the EU Artificial Intelligence Act) and UNESCO’s Recommendation on the Ethics of Artificial Intelligence. It concludes by identifying transparency, accountability, representative data, independent evaluation, and meaningful human oversight as central safeguards for rights-respecting AI governance.
