documents.abstract: This scoping review examines how AI literacy is connected to AI-supported problem solving in education. Drawing on 33 empirical studies published between 2020 and 2025, the review maps study characteristics, AI literacy dimensions, problem-solving types, and reported information behaviors. Findings show that AI-supported problem solving is a rapidly expanding interdisciplinary area, with the largest concentrations in STEM, computer science, and teacher education. AI tools most often supported design, decision-making, and diagnosis-solution problems. However, AI literacy was commonly represented through knowing and using AI, while the combined Evaluate and Create AI dimension and AI Ethics were less consistently represented, and verification and trust calibration were seldom explicitly analyzed. The review reframes AI literacy as question-centered information behavior (IB), emphasizing how learners identify information needs, formulate questions, check AI outputs, verify accuracy, and use information ethically. This perspective highlights good questioning as central to responsible AI-supported learning and problem solving.

Artificial Intelligence (AI) systems rely on algorithms to simulate human intelligence, learn from data, and support decision-making. Algorithmic literacy is relevant to LIS field because LIS has been at the forefront of promoting literacy at the intersection of people, technology, and information. The ACRL’s AI competency framework for academic library workers stipulates that library workers must be aware of the broad range of ethical issues with AI tools, including the design of “algorithms” (ACRL, 2025:p.4). It will be difficult for library educators, librarians, or any information professionals to be able to ask “good questions” on any AI systems driven by algorithms without possessing algorithmic literacy. While AI literacy is very important, it does not automatically translate into algorithmic literacy. Some of the questions that are yet to be addressed are: How is algorithmic literacy conceptualized in LIS field? What are the specific constructs that can be used to determine its implementation? How can it be assessed, and what are its ethical components beyond AI literacy? To answer these questions, we are synthesizing various LIS literature (within the last 5 years) on algorithmic literacy from four (4) academic databases (WoS, LISTA, Scopus, and ScienceDirect). The study is guided by PRISMA and a three-phase screening process using Yan et al.'s (2023) guidelines (title screening, abstract screening, and full-text review). One of the emerging patterns from the ongoing work at the full review stage is that algorithmic literacy is essential for managing online information services, supporting user engagement, and addressing ethical concerns in algorithmically mediated access.

documents.abstract: This study examined the relationship between crisis management strategies and organizational resilience among small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs) in General Santos City. Using a descriptive-correlational quantitative research design, the study assessed key crisis management dimensions and their influence on organizational resilience. Data were collected from 331 SME respondents and analyzed using descriptive statistics, Pearson’s correlation, and regression analysis. The findings revealed that SMEs demonstrated a high level of implementation of crisis management strategies, reflecting strong preparedness and proactive planning. Results further showed a very strong and statistically significant positive relationship between crisis management strategies and organizational resilience (r = 0.908, p < .001). This indicates that SMEs with more effective crisis management practices are better able to adapt, recover, and sustain operations during disruptions. The study concludes that crisis management strategies play a vital role in strengthening organizational resilience. SMEs that adopt structured and comprehensive crisis management frameworks are better equipped to navigate uncertainties and achieve long-term sustainability. It is recommended that SMEs further strengthen strategic planning, invest in employee training and technological resources, and continuously improve their crisis management systems to enhance resilience in a dynamic business environment.

documents.abstract: The emergence of generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) is transforming how students demonstrate their learning, challenging long-standing traditions about what counts as evidence of learning. While there are concerns that students may bypass essential learning processes by using AI to produce content, these tools may also present opportunities to enhance student learning. Grounded in pragmatism, this exploratory-sequential mixed-methods study examines how faculty in graduate programs in Library and Information Science assess student learning in the context of students' use of GenAI, while opening a discussion on how faculty can prepare to both address challenges and leverage opportunities presented by this technology. The first phase involved semi-structured interviews with 15 Master of Library and Information Science (MLIS) faculty members across ALA-accredited programs, analysed using reflexive thematic analysis. Findings informed the development of a survey instrument, which generated 206 faculty responses. The survey examined faculty perceptions, readiness, concerns, opportunities, assessment strategies, and best practices related to student use of GenAI. Findings highlight the nuanced and evolving nature of faculty responses to GenAI. Rather than framing AI solely as a threat or a tool for innovation, the results revealed a complex process of recalibrating assessment to foreground authentic learning, transparency, student reasoning, self-reflection, and to prepare graduates for AI-driven work environments. A central tension emerged between preparing students for an AI-driven workforce and preserving higher-order human capacities such as critical thinking, evaluation, ethical reasoning, and professional judgment. The study offers implications for assessment design, curriculum development, AI literacy, and workforce preparation in LIS education.

Loneliness has emerged as a growing concern among Chinese university students, and physical activity may represent a modifiable behavioral factor associated with loneliness; however, the psychological factors underlying this association remain largely underexplored. The purpose of this study was to examine the association between physical activity and loneliness, and to assess the mediating role of basic psychological needs among Chinese university students. A convenience sample of 1,195 university students in Zhejiang Province was surveyed to assess physical activity, loneliness, and basic psychological need satisfaction and frustration using the Global Physical Activity Questionnaire, the UCLA Loneliness Scale, and the Basic Psychological Need Satisfaction and Frustration Scale. Data were analyzed using IBM SPSS Statistics version 29.0 and PROCESS macro version 5.0. Results revealed that physical activity was negatively correlated with loneliness ( r = -0.374, p < 0.001) and basic psychological need frustration ( r = -0.402, p < 0.001) and positively correlated with basic psychological need satisfaction ( r = 0.297, p < 0.001). Mediation analyses indicated that both basic psychological need satisfaction and frustration independently mediated the relationship between physical activity and loneliness. Higher physical activity was associated with lower loneliness, with significant indirect effects through basic psychological need satisfaction and frustration. These findings suggest that basic psychological needs may help explain the association between physical activity and loneliness and may inform campus-based strategies aimed at addressing loneliness and supporting student mental health.

Under DepEd Order No. 3, s. 2026, Philippine basic education schools face an urgent mandate to integrate digital and smart technologies into instructional workflows. However, a significant operational divide persists in rural school districts between policy expectations and classroom readiness. This study evaluated the attitudes, instructional preparedness, and operational challenges of public elementary school teachers regarding Artificial Intelligence (AI) integration in Kasibu West District, leading to the development of a structured administrative intervention plan. Grounded in Everett Rogers’ Diffusion of Innovations Theory and the Technology Acceptance Model (TAM), a mixed-methods convergent parallel design was employed across all 23 public elementary schools in the district. Quantitative data were gathered from a mathematically determined sample of 120 teachers (N = 172, 100% response rate) selected via proportionate random sampling, using a structured 105-item 4-point Likert instrument. Content validity was established by a panel of three educational experts, and pilot testing with 25 NVSU MAEd graduate students (evaluated by an NVSU university statistician) demonstrated high internal reliability across sub-scales (Attitude α = .939, Preparedness α = .945, Challenges α = .710, Overall α = .910). Results revealed a High overall teacher attitude (Mean = 3.22, SD = 0.42), with Professional Efficiency ranking highest (Mean = 3.37). Instructional preparedness was likewise High (Mean = 3.05, SD = 0.40), led by Behavioral Intentions (Mean = 3.32) but constrained by low Professional Development and Training (Mean = 2.83). Operational challenges were High overall (Mean = 3.12, SD = 0.31), dominated by Technical and Infrastructure Barriers (Mean = 3.36). Inferential analysis yielded a statistically significant, very strong positive correlation between attitude and preparedness (r = .801, p < .001, n = 120), leading to the rejection of the null hypothesis. Qualitative thematic content analysis identified five core grassroots recommendations emphasizing hands-on Learning Action Cell (LAC) training, infrastructure hubs, DepEd-vetted tools, ethical policies, and administrative support. The empirical findings directly informed an expert-validated 4-Phase Administrative Intervention Plan Matrix to systematically address training deficits and upland digital friction.

Data physicalizations fabricated by 3D printers are limited in their ability to dynamically vary their form and tactile properties without refabrication, thereby hindering reusability. In particular, tactile properties on the surface of a physicalization (i.e., surface roughness ) cannot be dynamically adjusted as the data change. To address this limitation, we explore a novel method to increase the reusability of a data physicalization, namely perceived tactile modulation (PTM). Our method enables the perception of varying surface roughness levels on a static data physicalization through the use of virtual reality. By altering the visual roughness of the virtual model, we modulate the user’s perception of tactile roughness, thereby influencing how the physicalization is interpreted through touch and expanding the range of ordinal data values that can be encoded. We conducted two studies to design and evaluate this method. In the first study (N = 20), Just Noticeable Differences (JNDs) were established for perceivable visuo-tactile channels in virtual reality environments. The second study (N = 12) investigates the application of our method across two levels of interactive representation: static and interactive. Our findings show that PTM can reliably modulate perceived roughness in static physicalization, while its effectiveness for supporting dynamic, single-artifact updates (interactive encoding) requires further investigation. We present a series of recommendations for applying PTM techniques in data physicalization.

Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly used to support instructional planning, the development of learning materials, assessment, and student engagement. However, the extent to which science teachers are aware of, utilize, and pedagogically integrate AI tools in Biology teaching remains an important concern. This study determined the awareness, utilization, and pedagogical integration of AI tools among junior high school science teachers in the Division of Tagbilaran City, Bohol, and examined the predictive contribution of these variables to teachers’ perceived teaching effectiveness and ability to promote student engagement. A quantitative approach using a descriptive-predictive research design was employed. The respondents were 32 junior high school science teachers teaching Biology in public secondary schools, selected through total enumeration. Data were gathered using an adapted structured questionnaire administered through Google Forms and analyzed using frequency, percentage, weighted mean, and multiple linear regression. ChatGPT was the most recognized, currently used, and most useful AI tool. Teachers were aware of AI tools (M = 3.81), frequently utilized them in Biology instruction (M = 3.74), and occasionally integrated them pedagogically (M = 3.35). Their perceived teaching effectiveness and ability to promote student engagement were rated positively (M = 3.68). The regression model significantly predicted the outcome (R² = .603, F = 14.17, p < .001); however, only awareness was a statistically significant predictor (B = 0.450, p < .001). Utilization and pedagogical integration were not significant predictors. The findings informed a proposed professional development program to strengthen teachers’ AI literacy and support the effective, ethical, and curriculum-aligned integration of AI in Biology teaching.

documents.abstract: User intent disambiguation remains a key challenge in intelligent interactive systems. While it has been widely studied in dialogue systems in 2D interfaces, research on how intent disambiguation could be incorporated within Large Language Model (LLM) assisted editing workflows in immersive environments remains limited. Recent advances in LLMs create opportunities to leverage the immersive nature of virtual and augmented reality (VR/AR) environments to provide better disambiguation support. In this paper, we evaluate how traditional dialogue-based disambiguation can be augmented with spatially-anchored graphical previews to resolve ambiguous user commands in LLM-assisted parameter-driven editing workflows. A within-subjects study in which 24 participants completed complex geometry editing tasks in VR simulates scenarios where VR scenes are controlled by numerical parameters. Compared with the condition where disambiguation is not available, quantitative metrics and qualitative feedback indicate that a hybrid approach which combines clarification questions and graphical previews can support better interaction stability with fewer conversation rounds while improving user experience. These findings provide empirical evidence on the effectiveness of disambiguation methods in LLM-assisted editing of parameter-driven immersive scenes and inform design guidelines for future integration of LLMs in advanced VR/AR systems.

Artificial Intelligence-based Driver Behaviour Monitoring Systems (AI-DBMS) are used in heavy vehicle fleets to detect unsafe driving states and behaviours such as fatigue and distraction. However, limited research has examined risks across their lifecycle. This study used Hierarchical Task Analysis (HTA) to identify risks associated with AI-DBMS implementation. An HTA model of the AI-DBMS lifecycle was developed and validated through interviews with technology developers, fleet operators, regulators, and researchers. Participants selected HTA sub-goals relevant to their expertise and discussed risks and controls. Five risk categories were identified: (i) technology and system design, (ii) data-related, (iii) governance and regulatory, (iv) organisational, and (v) human and behavioural. Four control categories were identified: (i) governance and organisational, (ii) human-centred design and implementation, (iii) system assurance, and (iv) data management. Findings show AI-DBMS risks extend beyond technical performance and the driver-technology interface, highlighting the need for coordinated Human Factors approaches across the AI-DBMS lifecycle.

Effective conservation education must communicate ecological facts while also making distant environmental threats personally meaningful. Virtual reality (VR) may support this goal by allowing learners to experience such threats from a non-human perspective, yet it remains unclear whether embodied interactive VR primarily improves factual learning, affective engagement, or both. We present EcoShift VR, a dual-ecosystem experience in which users embody either a Sunda pangolin facing pollution and poaching or a blue shark facing pollution and bycatch. We evaluated EcoShift VR in a controlled 2 × 2 between-subjects study ( N = 40) comparing Medium (embodied interactive VR vs. lecture-style informational video) and Ecosystem (terrestrial vs. marine). As the media differed jointly in immersion, embodiment, agency, and interaction, their individual contributions cannot be isolated. All four conditions showed significant within-group factual knowledge gains after Holm–Bonferroni correction across the four paired comparisons, with no significant Medium effect on knowledge gain. Before multiplicity correction, 10 of the 13 Medium effects were statistically significant and favored embodied interactive VR, including nature connectedness, state empathy, perceived environmental awareness, and several curiosity and inquisitiveness measures. After Holm–Bonferroni adjustment across the 13 Medium comparisons, only the three state-empathy subscales (affective, cognitive, and associative) and the post-experience domain-specific curiosity composite remained statistically significant. A secondary within-condition analysis also identified a significant increase in nature connectedness for VR–Marine ( p Holm =.0053), although the overall Medium effect on nature connectedness did not survive correction. Other initially significant Medium effects were similarly attenuated after adjustment, while environmental-attitude gains remained directionally favorable to VR but inconclusive. These findings suggest that the broader embodied interactive VR experience can complement conventional environmental education, particularly by supporting empathy and conservation-oriented curiosity alongside factual learning.

Students increasingly rely on Large Language Models (LLMs) for academic advice, yet general-purpose models often lack institution-specific knowledge and can provide confident but inaccurate guidance. This creates risks for students and raises design questions about how universities should develop reliable, accountable, and maintainable LLM advising systems. This study evaluates three approaches for incorporating institutional knowledge into LLM-based advising systems: prompting, retrieval, and fine-tuning, compared across three open-weight models producing 48 configurations. Evaluation used an LLM-as-judge framework validated by student advisors serving as domain experts. Results show that the system prompt has the greatest impact on response quality, while retrieval provides complementary gains through source attribution. Fine-tuning produces only modest improvements. The LLM judge closely mirrors expert rankings, though it consistently assigns higher scores. These findings shift attention from model performance alone to the design and governance of maintainable, source-visible, uncertainty-aware advising systems embedded within human-led academic advising practice.

documents.abstract: Entry-level hiring in emerging startup ecosystems suffers from a critical structural flaw: an over-reliance on superficial resume keyword matching at the expense of workplace culture compatibility. Drawing on industry workforce data and qualitative insights synthesized from over 50 structured interviews with Chief Human Resources Officers (CHROs) and startup founders on the career podcast "Let’s Hear It From...", this paper examines the root causes of early-career attrition and Gen-Z workplace burnout. Industry benchmarks indicate that early-stage companies face a 43.7% rookie attrition rate—incurring ₹1.5 lakh to ₹3 lakh per bad hire—while 47.5% of startup employees report low psychological well-being. Qualitative findings reveal five recurring failure points among fresh graduates: mindset misalignment, inadequate organizational research, AI-assisted interview façades, theoretical baggage paired with low learning agility, and workplace etiquette deficits. To address this misalignment, this paper introduces the Human Energy Matching Framework, an automated, cognitive AI-driven methodology deployed via AlignCulture. By cross-referencing unstructured executive cultural baselines with multidimensional candidate behavioral assessments across dimensions such as Values Alignment, Learning Agility, Work Style Fit, and Purpose Alignment, organizations and higher education placement cells can transition from reactive keyword filtering to sustainable, wellness-driven talent integration. Author’s Note: Generative AI tools were utilized to assist in synthesizing qualitative transcripts from the "Let's Hear It From..." podcast archive and structuring the manuscript. All conceptual frameworks, empirical observations, and conclusions are the sole work of the author.

Introduction Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) is increasingly used in nursing education, but studies rarely evaluate task delegation explicitly. This review mapped evidence on educational tasks, contexts of use, and safeguards to inform boundaries for using large language models (LLMs) and delegating educational tasks. Methods This scoping review with critical evidence synthesis used JBI guidance for evidence mapping and PRISMA-ScR for reporting. MEDLINE, Scopus, and Web of Science were searched through 7 August 2026 for studies involving direct interaction between prelicensure nursing students and LLM-based systems. The review team extracted outcomes, risks, safeguards, and human oversight. The team proposed delegation statuses by considering the consequences of error, error detectability under specified safeguards, the need for human judgment, confidence in the evidence, and oversight feasibility. Results Of the 440 records screened, 46 studies comprising 47 educational application profiles were included. Of the 146 outcome records, 115 were favorable, 13 were mixed, 10 showed no difference, 6 were unfavorable, and 2 were unclear. Twelve studies (26.1%) reported at least one objectively verified error or event or an adverse educational outcome. Among the 118 safeguards, 100 (84.7%) were proposed or implemented without evaluation beyond implementation, five (4.2%) were evaluated for feasibility or acceptability, and 13 (11.0%) were evaluated for risk reduction. The proposed matrix comprises 16 task categories: eight conditionally delegable, five restricted to a supportive role, two unsuitable for automated delegation, and one with insufficient evidence. Conclusion The matrix offers a preliminary framework for task-specific decisions. Bounded knowledge support and low-risk formative feedback may be conditionally delegable with appropriate safeguards and oversight. AI should support clinical reasoning and care planning, whereas final grading, competence decisions, and ethical judgment should remain human responsibilities. The matrix requires validation and updating as direct evidence, particularly on safeguard effectiveness, becomes available. Clinical trial number Not applicable.

documents.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is renowned for its stochastic nature, where powerful computational performance is jeopardized by inconsistent, vague, and even flawed reasoning. When it comes to teaching MLIS students about serving information needs, seeking, use, and literacy, AI curricula present both opportunities and limitations to successful instruction. A research team explored a critical curriculum that draws distinctly from LIS examples of search trends, AI hallucination, and scholarly risks. Rather than a fixed and performance-based curriculum, this learning material aimed to bring MLIS students into conversations on AI use, risks, and even refusal. This work-in-progress study, which centers on student agency, contemplation, and critique, offers preliminary findings and opportunities for idea exchanges among LIS faculty.

Implicit user calibration and calibration-free eye-tracking methods have been explored to improve the usability of gaze-based interactions. However, these methods for regression- and model-based approaches typically require multiple observations or camera-display calibration. Therefore, we propose a binocular-constrained homography normalization method that enables calibration-free gaze estimation from a single observation without camera-display calibration. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first homography-based framework to incorporate calibration-free gaze estimation. For each eye, the corneal center and optical axis are estimated using a 3D eyeball model with a monocular camera, and the point-of-gaze is computed using homography transformations derived from both eyes. The proposed method achieved a mean horizontal angular error of 1.01° under the tested conditions. The experimental evaluations supported the feasibility of the proposed method and identified directions for further improvement.

As AI reshapes how people learn and create, questions arise about forms of knowledge that are embodied, practice-based, and difficult to articulate. This study examines how learners physically co-create with AI and what forms of tacit knowledge emerge through that process. It further investigates how emotions surface and are managed throughout AI-supported making. Through this examination, this study aims to holistically capture the cognitive, emotional, and behavioral dimensions of tacit knowledge acquisition in an AI-supported making environment. We designed and facilitated a pilot workshop centered on e-textile making with community members in Champaign-Urbana, Illinois in April 2026. E-textile was selected for its inherently tactile and embodied nature, offering a deliberate contrast to AI’s text-based, formalized mode of knowledge. Nine participants engaged freely with AI tools of their choice alongside human facilitators, creating a naturalistic environment where both forms of support coexisted. To capture the holistic process of cognition, behavioral patterns, and emotional responses, think-aloud protocols, observation, pre-post surveys, and interviews were used as data collection methods. Preliminary findings reveal no consensus on how AI supported ideation, process, or outcomes, suggesting that its role in tacit-knowledge-rich making is highly individual. Emotionally, participants expressed confidence, curiosity, and surprise throughout the workshops, while also navigating moments of stress and frustration. This study contributes to Library and Information Science understanding of how human-AI collaboration unfolds in spaces where knowledge is socially constructed and physically embodied. It further offers insight into the emotional experiences that emerge and are managed throughout AI-supported learning.

Artificial Intelligence (AI) is increasingly woven into Health and Physical Education (HPE) through motion analysis, wearable data, adaptive task design, automated feedback, and generative support for teachers. These developments are often associated with personalisation and, by extension, with the possibility of making learning more meaningful for individual students. This conceptual article questions that connection. Drawing on Kretchmar’s philosophy of meaning in movement, Meaningful Physical Education (MPE), and postdigital accounts of entangled pedagogy and technological mediation, it argues that meaningfulness is not a personalised output but a postdigital accomplishment. It emerges through embodied activity, relationships, material settings, cultural practices, interpretation, and time. Particular AI-supported arrangements may expand or constrain these conditions, but no technical adjustment can guarantee what an experience will come to mean. The analysis develops four tensions: personal relevance between dialogue and prediction; challenge between embodied negotiation and adaptive optimisation; fun, sociality, and delight beyond engagement analytics; and biographical meaning in relation to computational memory. It shows how personalised systems can also influence whose movements, preferences, and histories become visible and valued. The article concludes with five commitments for keeping meaningfulness open in postdigital HPE: interpretive openness, negotiated personalisation, embodied and relational attentiveness, collective possibility, and temporal and infrastructural humility.

Clinical artificial intelligence (AI) agents represent an emerging generation of AI systems. They extend conventional clinical decision support through goal-directed planning, tool interaction and adaptation of actions to intermediate results. Memory may support these functions but is not essential in every implementation. Human oversight is a safeguard for clinical deployment rather than an intrinsic capability. This short narrative review summarizes current evidence regarding the core architectural features, representative clinical applications, and primary implementation challenges of clinical AI agents. Recent studies indicate promising applications in diagnostic decision support, workflow automation, patient communication, and evidence synthesis. However, existing evidence remains largely based on technical validation studies, proof-of-concept systems, and conceptual frameworks, with relatively limited prospective evaluation in routine clinical practice. Key challenges include establishing reliable evaluation frameworks, ensuring process-level safety, developing effective governance structures, and generating robust clinical evidence to support implementation. Although technological progress is rapid, widespread adoption will require not only further technical advances but also rigorous clinical validation, transparent governance, and successful integration into healthcare workflows. Clinical AI agents may become useful components of multidisciplinary healthcare workflows, provided that future research addresses the remaining methodological and implementation challenges.

documents.abstract: As artificial intelligence (AI) becomes increasingly embedded in educational settings, learner heterogeneity can no longer be adequately described through single-variable comparisons. This study identifies learner profiles in AI-supported educational contexts using three theoretically grounded feature dimensions: AI self-efficacy, digital literacy, and cross-disciplinary integration self-efficacy. These dimensions were operationalized using eight indicators reflecting students’ AI-related confidence, digital information-processing competence, and integrative learning readiness. Based on 8,022 valid responses from eighth-grade students in the collaborative database of the Taiwan Assessment of Student Achievement: Longitudinal Study and the Taiwan i-Generation Panel Study, available from the Survey Research Data Archive, Academia Sinica, all input indicators were normalized using Z -score scaling to construct a standardized feature space for distance estimation. A two-stage clustering procedure was adopted. First, two-step cluster analysis was performed to compare candidate solutions based on Akaike Information Criterion and Bayesian Information Criterion values; subsequently, K -means clustering was conducted with the number of clusters fixed at six to estimate the final learner profiles. The results supported six profiles: high-scoring integrated; very low-scoring; AI-moderate, digitally weak; broadly below-average; digitally adequate, AI-integration weak; and near-average balanced. The profiles showed that learner heterogeneity was not organized along a simple high–low continuum but appeared as asymmetric configurations within the multidimensional feature space. Post-clustering analyses further showed that digital-literacy indicators and AI evaluation had the largest descriptive between-profile separations, and that cluster membership differed significantly by gender. The findings extend AI literacy research from average-based comparisons to cluster-based learner profiling and provide a basis for differentiated educational support and data-driven decision-making in AI-related educational settings.

documents.abstract: Generative Artificial Intelligence (GenAI) tools have become a standard in the User Experience (UX) & User Interface (UI) design workflows. There has been a shift in Artificial Intelligence (AI) systems reshaping how designers ideate, research, generate layouts, and refine interfaces. These AI systems promise speed and creativity within the UX workflows, but the increase in AI integration has raised questions around control and autonomy shift when they are used for design generation. In this thesis I have investigated the design outcomes when AI is positioned as a creative collaborator, influencing the decision authority and cognitive ownership. In this study, I have used research-through-design combining with auto-ethnography reflections, comparative user interface generation experiments (including Lovable AI-based website creations), and participatory engagements like Open Studio activity and a co-design workshop. The findings suggested that introducing AI early in the design process can lead the design to a specific framework, hierarchy and interaction pattern that narrow divergence. Designers can experience a drift in cognitive ownership while retaining their decision authority when authorship is distributed across prompts, iterations, and AI-generated drafts. In my experiments, AI outputs were polished and plausible but converged towards a similar structural layout. It reflected the influence of dominant pattern in their training data. This thesis argues for responsible integration of AI through careful timing, clear override options, and tools that make AI-driven influence visible, instead of rejecting it completely.

Current text-to-motion frameworks typically operate as a rigid, one-shot workflow where users are unable to intervene during the generation process, effectively limiting all refinement efforts to the iterative modification of the text prompt. This black-box process hinders iterative design, leading to inefficiency. Furthermore, natural language inherently suffers from ambiguity when describing fine-grained 3D motions, making it difficult for users to articulate their intent solely through text precisely. In this paper, we propose CoMotion , a real-time system that shifts the interaction paradigm from static text prompting to user-driven semantic steering. Instead of requiring users to restart the entire generation process for every modification, CoMotion operates directly within a discrete latent space by retrieving prompt-relevant atomic actions and presenting them as user-visible, adjustable controls. Through CoMotion , users can adjust semantic steering levels for these atomic actions to guide the generation toward their intent without the computational overhead of full text-to-motion model re-inference. Our approach provides a more diverse design pathway for the traditional one-shot text-to-motion generation process, enabling fine-grained, personalized motion control during generation. We validate our system using a standardized benchmark based on Large Language Models. Quantitative experiments demonstrate that CoMotion enables robust semantic correction and geometric diversity while maintaining the kinematic quality of the generated motions. Crucially, by transforming complex generative tasks into low-latency, interactive operations, CoMotion supports an interactive refinement workflow for the evaluated motion generation tasks.

Artificial intelligence (AI) is intensifying longstanding questions about the purposes of higher education, the authority of human judgment, and the university's obligations to society. This conceptual, theory-building article argues that AI competence is educationally insufficient when learners lack institutional conditions that make judgment consequential. Drawing on AI-literacy scholarship, ecological theories of agency, democratic education, the capabilities approach, and critical educational technology, it develops an ecological framework of Consequential Human Agency. The framework distinguishes individual capability from agency achieved in interaction with institutional authority, rights to contest and appeal, accountability, and material conditions of participation. Ethical, civic, professional, and leadership agency are treated as contexts of enactment rather than stages or measurable competencies. The article argues that universities are not benign guarantors of agency: as purchasers of platforms, assessment authorities, and users of surveillance and analytics, they can enable or constrain it. Higher education should therefore cultivate judgment while establishing institutional rights and procedures through which students and faculty can question, override, appeal, and help govern consequential AI-mediated decisions.

documents.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is transforming academic librarianship, requiring sustained ethical, evaluative, and instructional learning. Drawing on interviews with fourteen U.S. STEM academic librarians and scholarship on AI literacy and professional development, this paper examines how librarians develop AI competence through experimentation, peer networks, and personal knowledge management amid uneven institutional support. These conditions shift the costs of adaptation onto individual practitioners and raise concerns about equity, labor, and sustainability. The paper reframes continuing education as sociotechnical infrastructure for AI learning, identifies informal learning as structurally compelled labor, and proposes a role for library and information science (LIS) educators in designing ethical, collaborative, and sustained professional learning. Practice-based pathways, communities of practice, protected learning time, and institutional governance can support critical judgment as AI systems change.

documents.abstract: This article offers a philosophical reconstruction of the criteria for artistic mastery in the context of the proliferation of digital media and generative artificial intelligence. It challenges the tendency to equate mastery solely with technical proficiency, professional status, or the visual perfection of a work, while conversely reducing amateurism merely to aesthetic inferiority. The methodology integrates a phenomenological analysis of aesthetic experience, the hermeneutics of artistic decision-making, a media-philosophical perspective, and a critical examination of contemporary literature on the philosophy of AI. It is argued that generative technology alters not only the artist’s toolkit but also the modes of form emergence, the distribution of agency, and the processes of perception. The study proposes distinguishing between image generation, its artistic articulation, and the aesthetic event, processes that do not necessarily coincide. The novelty of this research lies in delineating three levels of an artistic work-technical generation, authorial articulation, and the aesthetic event and in conceptualizing mastery as a reflexively responsible capacity to organize the relationships between these levels, rather than as a mere sum of skills or a property of a finished artifact. Conclusions. Based on this, a multidimensional model of mastery is developed, encompassing intentionality, media literacy, reflexive selection, temporal depth, the productivity of aesthetic experience, and responsibility. It is demonstrated that the «human versus machine» dichotomy is less analytically productive than the distinction between the automated reproduction of the recognizable and responsible form-creation. Amateurism is interpreted as an open mode of participation in culture—one capable of evolving into mastery, independent of commercial or institutional legitimation.

Do servant leaders shape their followers’ vocational outcomes by the career support they provide or by helping followers find meaning at work? Drawing on self-determination theory, we test these two accounts, examining their competing effects on followers’ thriving at work, career satisfaction, and job search behaviors. Using the critical incident method (Study 1), we found that servant leaders influence vocational outcomes by deepening followers’ meaning at work, but not by providing career support. In a four-wave study (Study 2), both pathways were significant. A field study (Study 3) again supported only the meaning at work pathway, showing that meaning at work was most salient for followers with lower levels of work volition. An internal meta-analysis confirmed that both pathways carry a positive indirect effect in aggregate, but that the pathway through meaning at work is significantly stronger. Taken together, our results indicate that servant leadership is more vocationally consequential through the meaning followers internalize than the career support they receive, particularly among followers whose vocational agency is more constrained.

Generative and other AI-enabled technologies are accessible to small organisations, yet human–AI interaction (HAI) design guidance focuses on relatively direct user–system interaction. Rural HCI, community-centred design, participatory AI, digital inclusion, and social-enterprise research show that AI use is socially and organisationally situated. This late-breaking work develops the Micro-Social Venture (MSV) Framework through integrative conceptual synthesis of 55 selected sources. The framework connects six dimensions: Place, Community Agency, Organisational Mediation, Digital and AI Capability, Resource Conditions, and Governance and Social Outcomes. Its distinctive contribution is to treat the social venture as part of HAI itself: a community-embedded socio-technical intermediary through which AI is encountered, adapted, governed, and potentially refused. Five design propositions address place, collective agency, resource asymmetry, negotiated trust, and community stewardship. The framework is generative rather than predictive, offering HCI a diagnostic lens for examining community-embedded AI at geographic, organisational, infrastructural, and participatory edges.

documents.abstract: This article provides a theoretical foundation for assessing the analytical and critical competencies of future teachers in the era of generative artificial intelligence. It has been demonstrated that the limited reliability of automated AI-detection tools necessitates a shift from evaluating the final written product to a "process-over-product" diagnostic paradigm, while upholding the principles of academic integrity. Within the structure of an educator's analytical - critical competencies, the cognitive-diagnostic, didactic-design and reflexive-metacognitive components have been distinguished. A didactic model has been developed for designing AI - resistant assignments that focus on higher-order thinking skills, specifically "Analyzing", "Evaluating" and ″Creating″ according to Bloom's Taxonomy. The model incorporates the ″Three Zones ″ framework and utilizes three diagnostic formats: the analysis of contradictory pedagogical cases (Case Study), the cognitive auditing of AI-generated content (Reverse Engineering), and in-person, dialogue-based defense using the Socratic method (Socratic Defense). Furthermore, a criterion - based, multi-level rubric has been proposed comprising verification-analytical, didactic-adaptive, and metacognitive-authorial criteria to objectively assess students' professional agency and critical thinking.

This study investigates the determinants of job pressure among physical education lecturers in higher education institutions in Ho Chi Minh City, Vietnam, within the context of increasing academic demands and postpandemic transformations. Despite the growing importance of occupational stress in academia, limited research has focused specifically on physical education lecturers, particularly in developing countries. A quantitative research design was employed, with data collected from 220 physical education lecturers using a structured questionnaire. Reliability analysis (Cronbach’s alpha), exploratory factor analysis (EFA), and multiple regression analysis were performed using SPSS 20.0 to examine the relationships between the variables. The results indicate that job pressure is significantly influenced by five key factors, namely, the working environment (β = 0.760, p < 0.001), workload (β = 0.136, p < 0.001), role ambiguity (β = 0.096, p = 0.006), job performance (β = 0.091, p = 0.013), and workplace relationships (β = 0.075, p = 0.027). Among these, the working environment has the strongest effect, highlighting the critical role of organizational and environmental conditions in shaping job pressure. These findings contribute to the literature by confirming the multidimensional nature of job pressure and extending the application of person–environment fit theory, role theory, and transactional theory in the context of higher education in developing countries. Furthermore, the study provides empirical evidence from Vietnam, addressing a significant research gap. Practically, the results of this study suggest that universities should prioritize improving working conditions, optimizing workload distribution, and clarifying job roles to reduce job pressure and enhance lecturer performance. These implications are particularly relevant for institutions undergoing rapid transformation and quality assurance processes.

Mechanical ventilation (MV) is the recommended standard of care in many emergencies, yet its adoption by nursing professionals remains inconsistent. This research examines whether perceived clinical expertise is associated with emergency nurses' intention to use MV, directly and indirectly through trust in MV technology and attitude toward MV, and whether emergency severity moderates these associations. Emergency nurses (N = 236) were randomly assigned to one of four vignettes of decreasing acuity: cardiorespiratory arrest, severe hypoxaemia, chest trauma with respiratory compromise, and acute pulmonary oedema. Structural equation modelling showed that expertise was associated with trust and intention, trust with attitude, and attitude with intention; the serial indirect effect of expertise on intention through trust and attitude was significant. Because these constructs were measured concurrently, this effect is interpreted as an indirect association rather than as evidence of causal transmission. Higher severity strengthened the direct association between expertise and intention and weakened the association between trust and attitude, so that the serial indirect association declined as acuity increased. These findings are consistent with a shift from deliberative to automatic processing under time pressure and suggest that training should build expertise to automaticity for maximum-acuity scenarios while fostering trust in lower-acuity ones.

Digital health innovations are increasingly reshaping the delivery of healthcare and creating new possibilities for supporting the well-being of ageing populations. From telemedicine and remote patient monitoring to mobile health applications, wearable devices, and artificial intelligence-enabled services, these technologies can improve access to healthcare, strengthen disease management, and promote greater independence among older adults. However, their implications for the well-being of the aged population extend beyond clinical outcomes and involve psychological, social, behavioral, and functional dimensions of ageing. The paper adopted a secondary source of data. This theoretical study examines the relationship between digital health innovations and the well-being of older adults by synthesizing insights from existing conceptual and empirical literature and adopted successful aging theory as a framework to the study. The study conceptualizes digital health as an enabling mechanism through which older adults can participate more actively in managing their health and maintaining social connectedness. In conclusion, disparities in digital access, privacy concerns, technological complexity, and age-related are key to the health benefits of the aging population. The study recommends a conceptual perspective that integrates technological, individual, and social factors to explain how digital health innovations can contribute to healthier, more autonomous, and socially connected ageing. Keywords: Digital health, innovations, well-being, aged and population
topics: Aging, Elder Care, and Social Issues

documents.abstract: Public acceptance is widely regarded as a binding constraint on the contribution of nuclear energy to the green transition, yet claims that digital innovation will ease this constraint have rarely been examined against social science evidence. This topical review asks under what conditions digital innovation in nuclear energy systems, in particular digital twins, artificial intelligence (AI)-based predictive maintenance and the digitally supported design, manufacture and operation of small modular reactors (SMRs), can contribute to public acceptance of nuclear energy. The analysis draws on five strands of scholarship that are seldom brought into contact with the technical literature: risk perception research, cultural theory of risk, the deficit and engagement models of science communication, the social licence to operate, and socio-technical transitions theory, which serves as the integrating framework. Reading techno-optimistic claims through these lenses, the review identifies three structural barriers: a cybersecurity paradox, whereby the connectivity that enables digital safety functions simultaneously expands the attack surface; an economic gap, specific to SMRs, whereby projected cost reductions rest on serial-production assumptions that recent project experience has not supported; and a transparency fallacy, whereby information disclosure is expected to build trust although meta-analytic evidence links the benefit and risk perceptions associated with acceptance to trust rather than to knowledge. These barriers are argued to interact: cyber incidents could act as trust-destroying signal events, cost failures could undermine perceived institutional competence, and one-way transparency tools leave procedural justice concerns unaddressed. The review concludes that digital innovation is more likely to support acceptance when it is embedded in genuinely participatory engagement, when institutions demonstrably manage the new risks digitalisation creates, when economic claims are validated rather than promised, and when regulatory frameworks confer procedural legitimacy. Absent these conditions, digitalisation risks reproducing deficit-model assumptions that acceptance research has long found wanting.

This study examines the implications of digital policing and Artificial Intelligence (AI) adoption in the Nigeria Police Force for community trust and police legitimacy, with particular reference to Abia State. Anchored in Procedural Justice Theory, the study adopts a qualitative desk-review design, synthesizing peer-reviewed literature on digital policing, algorithmic decision-making, and Nigerian police-community relations. Abia State, with a 2006 census population of 2,845,380 spread across seventeen local government areas, provides a densely populated, predominantly urban and semi-urban context in which the legitimacy consequences of digital policing carry direct relevance for millions of residents. The review finds that digital tools carry real potential to strengthen policing capacity, but that their value for legitimacy depends less on technical sophistication than on whether their deployment is experienced by citizens as fair, transparent, and respectful. Evidence from Nigerian policing scholarship indicates that public confidence in the police remains persistently low, human discretion continues to compromise the neutrality of ostensibly objective digital systems, and police-public digital interaction in Nigeria remains predominantly one-directional rather than participatory. The study argues that without deliberate attention to voice, neutrality, and trustworthiness, the introduction of AI and digital infrastructure into Nigerian policing risks reproducing, rather than resolving, the legitimacy deficits that have long characterized police-community relations, and recommends that digital policing reform in Abia State be paired with institutional accountability and genuine community engagement. Keywords: Digital policing, digitalization, artificial intelligence, police legitimacy, community trust, procedural justice, Abia State
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: Most evidence for digital nudges comes from simple choice sets. We test whether they still work in information-dense financial interfaces and how AI assistants affect them. In an online experiment, 252 participants from Armenia managed a two-currency portfolio and made buy, hold, or sell decisions on dynamic time-series charts. Each participant saw five of ten manipulations under one of four AI conditions: no assistant or a neutral, biased, or debiasing assistant. Four manipulations shifted choices toward their target actions. A stated 70% chance of growth had the largest effect (+36.5 percentage points), followed by adding a third, decoy forecast to the two-forecast control set (+29.4 pp relative to that set), an upward price spike (+25.4 pp), and red highlighting of losses (+23.8 pp). The rest, including social proof and anchoring, had no significant effect. Paired nudges worked differently by direction: numeric and verbal cues mainly pushed buying, and the red cue pushed selling. A biased assistant roughly doubled the odds of the target action, while neutral and debiasing assistants had no detectable effect. Specific cues in the price chart still work in complex displays, and AI strengthens them more easily than it corrects them.

documents.abstract: In line with the explosion of public, political, and educational discourses around the incorporation of artificial intelligence (AI) in everyday life, researchers have recently invested a significant amount of time into exploring and theorizing the use of AI in qualitative data analysis. This proposed use of AI creates a theoretical friction with qualitative methodologists who foreground the interpretive (and essentially human) elements of this research praxis. To productively engage with this friction, authors--who span from being more quantitatively oriented to those who are considered Big Q Qualitative researchers--engaged in conversations with one another in a reflexive process of self-study. To help facilitate these conversations, all the authors explored CAILA, a qualitative analysis tool that uses AI to autonomously generate codes and themes from a text-based data set. Authors familiar with the tool spoke to the other three scholars who begrudgingly experimented with CAILA for the first--and last--time. Analysis of these conversations showed that participants felt that AI-based research tools could support menial aspects of qualitative analysis or help with coding of data based on established codebooks. However, the participants also found that tools like CAILA failed to provide meaningful interpretations of the data and stripped the humanistic components of qualitative research from the analysis process. These findings sit in opposition to the purported value of AI software, which emphasizes the efficiency of research processes. To this end, our findings position qualitative research as a human pursuit, asserting that the slow pace of the coding processes provides the space needed for researchers to develop new ideas and meaning from bodies of text. We contribute to the ongoing conversation about using AI for qualitative data analysis by providing fresh perspectives from Big Q Qualitative methodologists and inviting the field to think more deeply about the qualitative research process.

Artificial intelligence (AI) now underpins FinTech services that support digital financial inclusion and sustainable economic growth, yet AI-enabled fraud threatens users' trust in this innovation. Some users intend to discontinue AI-enabled FinTech services even when they are satisfied and habituated, a pattern that traditional continuance explanations do not explain. This study examines a Dual Evaluation Mechanism in which discontinuance intention forms through an internal path (confirmation, satisfaction, and habit) and an external path (vicarious exposure to AI fraud and perceived AI fraud risk), and tests whether perceived AI fraud risk moderates the relationship between habit and discontinuance intention. The study employs cross-sectional survey data from 507 Indian users of AI-enabled FinTech services, analyzed with partial least squares structural equation modeling and complemented by predictive, importance-performance, endogeneity, and necessary condition analyses. The results show that confirmation raises satisfaction (β = 0.648), satisfaction raises habit (β = 0.578), and habit lowers discontinuance intention (β = −0.330). Vicarious AI fraud exposure raises perceived AI fraud risk (β = 0.588), which raises discontinuance intention (β = 0.507), and the interaction between risk and habit is positive (β = 0.174); all paths are significant at p < 0.001. The model explains 39.9% of the variance in discontinuance intention and outperforms the indicator-average benchmark in out-of-sample prediction. The findings suggest that all six hypotheses are supported, that perceived AI fraud risk is the most important predictor of discontinuance intention (0.507) and weakens the protective effect of habit, and that no construct is a strong necessary condition for discontinuance (d ≤ 0.163). This registration documents the protocol for a systematic full-text review and verified evidence map of dynamic trust in artificial intelligence. The review examines how trust in AI changes over time or in response to interaction evidence, including reliability and error exposure, explanation and transparency, confidence and uncertainty cues, trust violation, and trust repair. The current project began with a Web of Science-derived corpus and will be transparently updated through final eligibility verification, independent coder checking, quality appraisal, and, where evidence permits, focused quantitative synthesis. This registration is reported as a transparent protocol record for the final review stage rather than a fully prospective preregistration, because initial corpus assembly and manuscript drafting had already begun before registration.

documents.abstract: This thesis examines how artificial intelligence (AI) can be used effectively in teaching English as a foreign language. It reviews the theoretical grounds for AI-supported instruction and describes five pedagogically sound applications: automated writing feedback, conversational practice with chatbots and voice assistants, adaptive personalization, generative AI for materials development, and AI-assisted assessment. It also considers risks such as over-reliance, accuracy problems, and ethical concerns. The analysis suggests that AI is most effective when it complements, rather than replaces, the teacher, when it is tied to clear learning objectives, and when learners are trained to use it critically.

Artificial intelligence (AI) is being adopted in university teaching faster than evidence on its instructional value is being consolidated. This systematic review examined whether AI-based interventions improve achievement, engagement, satisfaction, and knowledge retention among undergraduate and graduate students relative to conventional instruction. Following PRISMA 2020, seven queries in SciSpace, Google Scholar, and PubMed, run on September 23, 2026, identified 902 records. After deduplication and a relevance-ranking cut-off, 500 records were screened, 82 reports were assessed for eligibility, and the 80 provisionally eligible reports were verified against publisher, index, or repository records. Reports that could not be verified (n = 52), proved ineligible (n = 4), or existed only as non-peer-reviewed preprints (n = 2) were excluded, leaving 22 peer-reviewed reports: 14 primary comparative studies and eight meta-analyses. Evidence was integrated through a structured narrative synthesis without meta-analysis, using design-based robustness indicators. Five primary studies were randomised. Meta-analyses restricted to higher-education students reported moderate effects on achievement in college populations (Hedges’ g = 0.32–0.53) and inconsistent effects in medical education (SMD = 0.27–2.06); broader-population syntheses were treated as contextual only. Primary studies were favourable when AI was embedded in structured pedagogical designs, whereas comparisons with well-designed conventional or human instruction often showed no advantage, and unguided generative AI use improved immediate performance more than retention or transfer. Given the small, largely non-randomised evidence base and declared departures from standard search practice, the evidence supports only tentative, design-dependent claims about AI in higher education.

documents.abstract: Generative artificial intelligence has entered Ethiopian higher education faster than pedagogical frameworks for its use. This study examined the effects of a blended model combining AI-assisted feedback with teacher-led instruction on EFL students’ academic writing development and writing self-efficacy. A one-group pre-test–post-test quasi-experimental design with an embedded qualitative strand was used. Thirty-seven third-year students of the Department of English Language and Literature at Salale University, enrolled in the Intermediate Writing course, received ten weeks of blended instruction in which AI tools supplied immediate draft-level feedback and the teacher supplied genre, content and revision instruction. Teaching materials were modified from the existing course textbook rather than newly prepared. Writing was assessed with an adapted analytic rubric and self-efficacy with the Second Language Writer Self-Efficacy Scale. Paired-samples t-tests showed significant gains in overall writing, from M = 51.38 to M = 64.22, t (36) = 10.00, p < .001, d = 1.64, and in writing self-efficacy, from M = 2.84 to M = 3.73, t (36) = 9.33, p < .001, d = 1.53. Gains were largest for content and organization and smallest for mechanics. Writing and self-efficacy gains correlated moderately, r = .46, p = .004.

Artificial Intelligence has achieved significant advances in perception, language generation, reasoning, and decision-making. However, current Artificial Intelligence systems primarily optimize task performance and remain limited in their ability to account for emotional context, ethical considerations, and long-term human well-being. Existing research on Emotional Intelligence, Affective Computing, Compassionate Artificial Intelligence and Theory of Mind addresses different aspects of this challenge, but these capabilities have largely been studied independently. We propose Emotional Superintelligence as a new computational paradigm that integrates contextual emotional understanding, compassion, ethical reasoning, human-value alignment, and well-being-oriented decision-making into a unified Artificial Intelligence framework and introduce a five-layer model. Our Model adopts a functional view of emotional understanding, focusing not on whether an Artificial Intelligence system subjectively experiences emotions, but on how effectively it interprets emotional context and uses that information to make responsible and compassionate decisions. Potential implementation pathways for Large Language Models and autonomous systems are recommended along with applications in diversified domains such as healthcare, education, governance, and Human-Artificial Intelligence interaction. We also identify key challenges concerning multi-modal emotion understanding, emotional bias, manipulation, privacy, human oversight, and long-term well-being. By integrating emotional and ethical capabilities into the Artificial Intelligence decision process, Emotional Superintelligence reframes intelligent-system development from task optimization alone towards responsible human flourishing and provides a research agenda for future compassionate and socially beneficial Artificial Intelligence.

This paper presents an end-to-end AI-assisted framework for the automated generation of hazard and operability (HAZOP) reports to address key challenges of current HAZOP practices, including time consumption, human bias, and knowledge loss. The framework consists of four modules, each employing a set of artificial intelligence (AI) models to support the generation of HAZOP notes, including deviations, causes, consequences, safeguards, and recommendations. The First module assesses the degree of similarity (expressed in 3 levels: high, medium, or low) between current and past piping and instrumentation diagram (P&ID) nodes using object, location, and functional similarity metrics. Object and location similarities are computed using the detected classes and bounding boxes coordinates obtained from YOLO models, while functional similarity is derived from node descriptions generated by large language models (LLMs). These metrics are then combined to compute the P&ID Node Similarity Index (PNSI), which determines the similarity level to guide subsequent analysis. For the high level, the associated HAZOP notes are directly retrieved and reused. For the medium level, the second module employs BERTopic to identify dominant topics from retrieved HAZOP notes. For the low level, the third module employs retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) and domain-adapted embeddings to enhance the reliability of generated HAZOP notes. The three modules, referred to above, are integrated into a Streamlit-based web interface to facilitate their respective applications to automatically generate HAZOP reports. The framework is tested primarily using a dataset of 510P&ID node images, 6,120 HAZOP notes and 1,140 incident investigation reports collected from diverse sources. The P&ID nodes were annotated using Roboflow , resulting in 13,780 labeled objects across 21 classes. The YOLOv8x model achieved 82.4% precision, 74.8% recall, and 79.2% mAP@50. Three P&ID nodes were used to illustrate how the modules interact under different similarity conditions. The results demonstrate the effectiveness to benefit from past HAZOP knowledge, thereby capturing the embedded experience and reducing the time required to perform HAZOP studies and prepare related reports.

Concurrent engineering (CE) is a process that integrates product, process, manufacturing, service and life cycle design decisions into concurrent activities instead of sequential activities. Not only is its potential related to team composition of experts, but also to how teams share knowledge, deal with dependencies, communicate design intent and address trade-offs in a time-critical environment. This manuscript builds upon the idea that a conscious application of group design can enhance innovation and accelerate development time and first-time-right product performance, but that group design can also lead to coordination overhead, group-think, conflict, and more iterations. It builds an integrative conceptual framework that connects collaborative design practices to design process results via knowledge integration, shared situational awareness, decision quality and capability for change management. The framework categorizes the following: structural conditions (team composition, task interdependence and governance); process mechanisms (communication, shared digital representations, constructive conflict and design reviews); enabling infrastructure (CAD, product data management, product life cycle management, simulation and digital-thread capabilities); and outcomes (novelty, quality, rework, lead time and life cycle value). There are three research questions and testable hypotheses that are stated. A future systematic or scoping review is proposed, with a transparent, reproducible review protocol, and a mixed-method empirical approach to testing the review protocol without suggesting that data have already been gathered. The paper presents a multilevel model, operational definitions, measurement ideas, boundary conditions and a research agenda for collaborative design in modern CE, such as distributed teams, AI-supported design and Industry 5.0 centered CE. As no original experiment, survey or interview data set is provided for this manuscript, the article instead offers a conceptual synthesis and proposed research protocol instead of fabricated empirical findings.

Work-related musculoskeletal disability often becomes visible only after exposure has continued long enough to produce lost time, medical restrictions, or workers’ compensation claims. This article argues that states should adopt pilot programs for technology-assisted ergonomic risk detection because earlier task evidence can help identify hazardous work design before preventable strain becomes disabling. Using policy synthesis, legal and regulatory analysis, public health evidence, ergonomic research, and a Christian public ethics lens, the article proposes a state-level pilot model for warehousing and delivery work, health care support, and long-term care, manufacturing, and related material handling operations. The model combines mobile task observation, accepted ergonomic scoring methods, worker symptom reporting, corrective action tracking, privacy-protected dashboards, validation standards, worker participation, and human review. Virginia serves as the illustrative policy setting because its occupational safety program and workers’ compensation framework create a useful context for testing exposure documentation before broader regulatory reform is considered. The article also addresses implementation risks by distinguishing prevention from surveillance, productivity discipline, medical diagnosis, and automatic claim decisions. It recommends phased state pilots, responsible use guidance from occupational safety agencies, worker privacy rules, incentive structures for documented corrective action, and continued evaluation of feasibility, language access, worker trust, and injury outcomes. Properly governed, technology-assisted ergonomic risk detection can strengthen prevention, support fairer evidentiary records, and preserve worker dignity while helping public agencies and employers respond to hazardous task design before harm becomes permanent.

documents.abstract: The AI guidelines, developed within the EU’s EL PACCTO 2.0 programme, set an ethical framework for judges and prosecutors in Europe, Latin America and the Caribbean who use Artificial Intelligence. Their core principle is that AI may assist but must never decide, so every decision stays with a human who is fully accountable for it. Judges and prosecutors must verify every AI output, keep confidential and judicial data out of public chatbots, and use only systems with the highest cybersecurity standards. Institutions should publicly disclose which AI systems they use and favour secure, locally hosted tools that use resources sparingly. Ongoing training and binding codes of conduct should help them use AI critically and avoid automation bias. In criminal justice, the guidelines add stronger safeguards for the presumption of innocence, the rights of the defence and the right to challenge evidence produced with AI.

Introduction: Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) can minimise large language model hallucinations while supporting self-regulated learning. We evaluated the impact of student engagement with a grounded RAG-AI tool (Google NotebookLM) on formative and internal assessment scores in undergraduate pathology, validated a 3-item AI Disclosure Form, and explored cognitive adoption barriers. Methods In a 12-week longitudinal study using an interrupted time series design, Phase II medical students (N = 211) received curated NotebookLM modules alongside core lectures. Students completed weekly quizzes, a 3-item disclosure form assessing the frequency, application mode, and trust in the AI resources, and end-of-study mixed-method questionnaires. Longitudinal cohorts were classified into High, Low, Inconsistent, and non-usage groups, with differences evaluated via ANOVA. Results The 3-item disclosure form demonstrated high reliability. The average scores of formative quizzes (p = 0.656) and summative internal exams (p = 0.961) did not differ significantly between the engagement groups. However, there were notable differences in performance during some of the dense, complex sections (Lung, p < 0.001; Renal, p < 0.001). Frequent users used active Socratic chat and self-quizzing to handle high cognitive demands. In contrast, inconsistent users showed "cognitive flight" under stress, and non-respondents scored significantly lower (24.83 ± 13.76). Conclusion A standalone RAG-AI tool does not automatically improve the overall performance of a group. Instead, it helps manage cognitive load during demanding modules for learners who are good at self-regulated learning. Future use needs structured workflows within a Learning Management System and training for prompt verification.
